Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 99, to amend the Exchequer Court Act. He said: The purpose of the Bill is simply to extend the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court so as to enable it to determine questions purely and simply of value. In the past there have been instances where the situation that arose was either that some

party or parties put before the Government or some department of the Government a claim with regard to which there could be no room for debate or discussion as to the existence of the claim, hut which was of such a nature that the quantum to be paid could not be agreed upon and was not easy of determination, or that it having been deemed proper that certain property or properties belonging to the Crown should be disposed of by sale or lease or otherwise, the parties concerned and the department concerned were not able to determine what would be the precise value. The purpose of the Bill is to add a clause to the Exchequer Court Act enumerating the matters with regard to which that Court shall have jurisdiction and to add a clause giving it jurisdiction for the purpose of determining the value in cases such as I have referred to. The present difficulty is that in such cases there is no case proper that comes under any of the cases enumerated in the existing section.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to move the adjournment of the House, and before doing so, I want to state that I have given you very short notice. I have given the leader of the Government no notice at all, and I realize that I am perhaps trespassing upon the good nature of the House in taking this course, but my reasons are as follows: A matter occurred this afternoon at the sitting of the Royal Commission when Mr. Johnston was prohibited from cross-examining witnesses on the ground that the scope of the commission was not broad enough to permit of his doing so. I wish here in the most emphatic manner to state that I do not wish to be considered as casting any reflections whatever upon the decision of the commissioners. I simply want to state the facts as accurately as I can. Mr. Johnston rather persisted in the matter, and finally the commission made the statement that it might be advisable to apply to Parliament in order that further powers might be given to them. The only way that I could do so would be to move the adjournment of the House in order to discuss the matter, and the discussion on that motion, as my hon. friends know, would

be a discussion only of the matter itself and, of course, would not decide what might take place in the future. I did not leave the rooms of the commission until ten minutes past one o'clock and I had no time whatever to see anybody. As the House met at two o'clock, I simply handed to Your Honour a very rough draft of my proposal and I had no opportunity of communicating the matter to my right hon. leader or to the Government side of the House.

I may say in general
terms, that, of course, there would be no objection to the adjournment of the House being moved for the discussion of any question of public importance. My hon. friend presents a statement of what he claims to be the facts as presented at the commission about one o'clock

We have not the exact statement as made by the commissioners and the reasons given for their refusal, and I think my hon. friend should at least be satisfied to allow the matter to stand until to-morrow when we shall be pleased to facilitate any proposal he wishes to make with respect to the adjournment of the House for the discussion of the matter, as we shall then have a report before us.

'Mr. CARVELL: Yes, That was written in a great hurry.

I can only repeat wha/t I said a moment ago, that, in view of the fact that the House would not be in possession of the facts of the case and the actual statements made by the commission giving their reasons for the refusal, whatever they may have been, I think my hon. friend from Carleton will appreciate that he should not press the motion until tomorrow, when, I assure him, everything will be done to facilitate the bringing of it before the House with a view to having the discussion he desires.

I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Doherty, the motion standing in .the name of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), as follows:
That on and after Saturday next, the sixth instant, and on Saturdays until the end of the present Session, the House shall meet at two o'clock in the afternoon; and the order of precedence on Saturdays shall be the same as on Thursdays.

I would suggest to the hon. gentleman leading the Government, that he do not propose this motion to cover next Saturday. The reason ie that a great many members, believing that this would be the last free Saturday they would have, have made arrangements to go home and fix up business to stay here' through next week, at least until the session is concluded. In addition to that, there is a good deal of correspondence in connection with the two railway propositions which hon. members wish to digest, and for this they have no time but Saturday. I would suggest that the motion be changed to refer to a week from Saturday.

I desire to register a very
mild protest against the unnecessary prolonging of the session. We have been sitting here now for a good many months. I think it has been in the minds of many hon. members on both sides of the House that this motion would be moved to-day, or that it ought to be moved. I cannot conceive of any good excuse or reason which can be urged to prevent the House from expediting the business of the session so that we may arrive at the earliest prorogation possible.

In answer to the hon.
member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), I may say that this motion was proposed by reason of the fact that, as he can see, there is evidence on both sides of the House of a strong desire that the session should come to an end. The Government are doing everything possible to facilitate the work and to meet the wishes of the members on both sides of the House with the view of bringing the session to an end. I hope my hon. friend will see that the desire of hon. members on both sides of the House is respected to this extent and that we shall endeavour to get on with business on Saturday. If my hon. friend wishes the railway proposals to stand, we can take up other matters in connection with the Estimates, and clean up the work which is still left. By that means we should be able to close the session next week. If hon. gentlemen are well disposed to the carrying out of the business of the House, there is no reason at all, that I can see, why it should not be possible to prorogue in a week or ten days. .

I was not speaking for
myself at all, but for several members who have spoken to me in regard to this very motion. While hon. members opposite are not saying anything, those who are opposed to it are saying something. With reference to the expedition of business, I say that there has never been a session during which I have been in this House in which the Estimates have gone through with so much expedition as they have this session. There can be no doubt about that. The minister will remember that there is one very important item of legislation which is constantly before the public and the press,

and which has not yet been brought down. We have begun to sit at two o'clock on week days, and now it is proposed to sit on Saturdays, and that piece of legislation is not yet before the House. I submit that even before we decided to meet at two o'clock the programme of the Government, as is customary, should have been laid before the House. Then we would have known what business was to be transacted. As it is, we do not know. A new Bill was brought down to-day by the Government, an amendment to the Exchequer Court Act. I do not think it is very serious, but to-morrow there may be half a dozen new Bills brought down.
The Prime Minister gave notice of that Bill three or four days ago.

He mentioned in a discussion that there would be an Exchequer Court Bill, but that does not alter the effect of my statement. The Prime Minister may say to-morrow that a Bill will be brought down the next day. The Government ought to tell us what its programme is, and then we can sit mornings, nights, and Sundays, if necessary, if the Government want to get through. If it be true that the Government is keeping back an important piece of legislation till the last moment, I do not think it is fair to the House to rush the business through on Saturdays until they tell us their programme. It has always been done heretofore.

There may be some ground for my hon. friend's statement in respect to further legislation, and while I am anxious that this motion should be agreed to, as I trust it will be, my hon. friend can depend upon it that the Prime Minister will make a statement to-morrow of all the legislation that is to be brought before the House.

I hope we can depend
on everybody being here on Saturday.
I hope so.

The members from the
East and West have to be here.
Motion agreed to.

I think' those powers were leased from the local Government.
I discussed that with the chief engineer, and he told me it was from the local Government and not from our department.

It would be interesting, in view of what has taken place lately, to know whether it was the Federal or Provincial Government that leased those powers. I am inclined to think it was the Provincial Government, and that they are simply getting back the powers which they themselves leased.
Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada -to pay expenses in connection with cases before them, $25,000.
That is the usual annual vote for that purpose.

I noticed in the press some time ago that an application had been made by the Canadian Northern Railway for permission to reduce the rate on, I think, oil in some parts of the West; that complaint was made by the other rail-

ways against the reduction, and that the Board of Railway Commissioners refused to allow the Canadian Northern Railway to make the reduction. It was an unusual position for the board to take. I have always supposed that if a railway was ready to carry goods at a reduced rate, the Board of Railway Commissioners would allow it to do so. I was a little surprised to see that statement in the press. Could the minister tell me anything about it?

I saw that statement in the press. As the hon. member knows, the Board of Railway Commissioners have a power to fix rates on the several railways. When the Board fix them the railways must put them in force to the public. They have the right, as I understand the law, to prevent the railways from making rates lower than the figures at which they fix them. I suppose this was done in order that no injustice might be done to some other railway. A large corporation, like the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern, might fix lower rates to injure some smaller railway, and for that reason the Board of Railway Commissioners have power to see that no injustice is done to any railway operating in or near the territory through which another railway passes. That is the law, as I understand it.

I know something about that case. It was not a rate on oil; it*was a rate given to the Standard Oil Company, or the Canadian branch of the Standard Oil Company, to carry to the West an amount of manufactured steel for the purpose of the construction of buildings to provide a distribution plant in the Prairie Provinces. This steel came in from across the line and the company made application for a rate which would approximate the manufacture in transit rate, just as wheat is given a rate, allowed to be unloaded, made into flour, and then taken in. Application was made to the Board of Railway Commissioners for the disallowance of the rate given. If it had been a universal rate which applied to any appreciable amount of business, the Board of Railway Commissioners might not have given the same decision, but it was evidently in the nature of a rebate to a particular company for a particular amount of business and so against the intendment of our Railway Act and absolutely against the principle of the InterState Commerce Act by which rebating is made a crime. I think the Board of Railway Commissioners took the ground that
practically, if not technically, it was a violation of the spirit of the Act in that it gave special privileges to one company which practically could not be taken advantage of by any other company.

When I drew the attention of the minister to the matter I did not have the reference, but I have it now and perhaps it will do no harm for me to read it to him:
In a decision given out Saturday, the Railway Commission refused to allow the Canadian Northern railway freight rate cut on steel from Toronto to Regina.
I was mistaken when I said it was oil.
It was an oil company.

It had something to do with oil then.
The rate was a special one given the Imperial Oil Company, which is building a big refinery at Regina. The crude steel is being obtained in Pittsburg. American railways offer a rate of 75 cents from Smoky City to Regina. The company is having the steel fabricated at Sarnia and is shipping it to that point and from there to Regina. The G.T.R. and C.P.R. held out for a rate of $1.04. The oil company was looking for a 75 cent rate and the C.N.R. accommodated them with a rate of 585 cents per hundred pounds from Toronto to Regina. With the local rate from Sarnia to Toronto, this made a through rate of 75 cents from Sarnia to Regina.
There was a united kick from the older railways, backed up by Winnipeg manufacturers. For the first time, perhaps, the Railway Commission refused to allow a railway to reduce its rate.
You will see that the American railways were willing, provided the material was fabricated in the United States, to ship it to Regina for 75 cents a hundred, but the Canadian railways held out for $1.04. The Canadian Northern, for some reason, were not willing to do it for less than 75 cents. I see no reason why they should not have been asked to carry the goods at the rate the American railways were ready to give them. However, that is the case.
Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada -maintenance and operation of, including $800 for Clyde Leavitt, as chief fire inspector, $178,350.
What are Mr. Leavitt's duties in connection with the commission?
Mr. Leavitt is the chief fire inspector for the commission. His duties are in connection with fires along the railways which the commissioners are obliged to investigate.

They do not give him
any money for doing that kind of work.
$800 ie what the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners recommends.
He possibly has some other position and this is to be paid him by the commissioners?
He is employed in the Interior Department and this is in addition to hie salary in that department.
Both departments pay him.
Yes.

I Temember that certain powers were given the Board of Railway Commissioners with reference to the prevention of fires. The Board, if I remember correctly, in connection with an agreement with the railway companies and the Chairman of the Conservation Commission, issued some orders in reference to fire protection along different lines. The Canadian Pacific burn oil going through the mountains.
Yes.

That was suggested by the Board of Railway Commissioners and the British Columbia Government, and I understand that really an order wa6 not issued. In connection with the construction of the Transcontinental through New Brunswick, I think Mr. Flemming came to Ottawa, there was a consultation and we arrived at a decision by which the Transcontinental and the New Brunswick Government acted in unison for the protection of forests during the construction of the railway. That railway was taken over by the Government and it passes through some very valuable property in New Brunswick and in other provinces as well. What steps are the Government taking in reference to the protection of forests in the country through which the Transcontinental is operating?

The several provinces have their own fire protection service. The hon. gentleman knows the system which is in force on the Intercolonial railway. I think they have tank cars located at different points that they can run along the line and then sectionmen are supposed to watch for fires. In a part of New Brunswick, and in Quebec, there was a private company which owned a large forest and they were paid a certain amount by the Transcontinental Railway Commission and, I

think, by the New Brunswick Government, the company paying a certain portion of the cost. This matter came before me some time ago, and a return was brought down the other day on the subject. We are following the same policy on the Transcontinental since we took it over, as on the Intercolonial; the one policy applies to the whole system. We have tank cars located at different points, and we are not paying anything for outside protection against forest fires occurring along the line.

There has been enough
timber lost in Canada through forest fires to keep us running for a good many years, and we are only now beginning to wake up to the necessity of being more careful. The Government, which has now a pretty big mileage under operation, ought to be a model in its precaution against fires occurring along the line of railway. The Interior Department with their fire rangers assist the Government in this respect. If I remember correctly, legislation was passed some years ago, at the instance of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and with the consent of all the railways, after consultation requiring the leading ' railways to station men at certain intervals along their road solely for the purpose of protection against fires. By a little expenditure in this direction a great amount of money may be saved. In British Columbia alone there has been destruction of timber to an extent that, at present prices, would startle the world. I think that what gave rise to the legislation was the number of complaints that had been made against the various railway companies, including the Intercolonial, for having started so many fires. I admit at once that I think the Intercolonial is blamed for a good many fires for which it is not responsible.
That is right.

I should not like to admit that the Intercolonial has caused all the fires of which it has been accused. A good deal can be done, and I imagine is being done to prevent forest fires, by using improved .smoke-stacks, careful firing, and all that kind of thing. A few years ago the private companies, and possibly the Intercolonial, endeavoured to run their trains with engines of too small a capacity, with the result that at the least bit of an incline open went the door, the coal was shovelled in, and a streak of sparks, and fire almost, shot out of the smoke-stack. I suppose that to-day the

Board of Railway Commissioners insists upon the latest improvements being used by the companies, particularly in districts where there is valuable timber, and I think that that is one of the most important duties the Board of Railway Commissioners could have at the present time.

There is some legislation empowering the Board of Railway Commissioners to give special attention to protection against forest fires throughout Canada, and I agree with the hon. member that it is a matter of great importance. The forests of Canada are a great asset, and everything should be done to protect them. I believe that the present
3	p.m. regulations are good, and are being acted upon. I remember discussing this matter of fire protection with the Hon. Mr. Cochrane and Mr. Gutelius, and Mr. Cochrane gave instructions that the same precautionary measures were to be taken on the Transcontinental as on the Intercolonial. There should be only one system of fire protection for the whole Government railways. Some one suggested to me that the question of fire protection on the Government railway system should be under the Board of Railway Commissioners. I did not care to take that matter up until the minister was here. My own view is that if you are putting the question of fire protection under the Board of Railway Commissioners you may as well put the whole thing under them.
Do you mean the Intercolonial?
The whole Government system.
I did not suggest that.

No, but that is how it strikes me. The minister and I think that if the present law in regard to fire protection is good for the private railway companies it is good for the Government railway sy'stem, and if it is carried out on the Government railway system I think that should meet the wishes of all concerned. That, I understand, is the system that is being carried out on the Government railways. Our own employees are doing the work, but in addition to them we have protection from the Interior Department, which, to a certain extent, looks after forest fires throughout the Dominion.
Their work is mostly in the West.

Probably it is. Then each local Government has its fire rangers and fire protection service, so that not only the Dominion Government, but the local Governments and all the railways realize the great importance of protection against forest fires, and are doing what is necessary in that respect.
What system is employed for protecting the railway property itself, in case a fire breaks out at the station?
There is no fire insurance.
Is there any protection against fire?

It must depend, of course,
upon the local service in any municipality. If fire should break out, say, in any of the small stations along the line, we have no special fire protection.
The matter would be all right in a town where there is a fire engine, but there are numerous places along the line where there is no municipal fire protection whatever.

At large places we have our tank service and hose from our tanks along the line, but in small places where there is no special fire protection service, we could not do anything other than have, say, a chemical extinguisher.

A couple of years ago an arrangement was made with the people at Matapedia and the railway by which they could use the water of an old reservoir, and at the time I asked that more hose be put into the station in case fire should break out on the Intercolonial or in the village. The place is huddled up close to the Intercolonial property and there have been a couple of fires there in the past. The last complaint made last year was that the hose in the station was not long enough to reach the houses in the village. The Minister of Railways promised at that time that he would look into the matter. I also asked him if arrangement would be made with the residents of the localities by which they could use the water for domestic purposes.	*

I was present when the
matter came up. I gave instructions to the general manager to see that the hose was supplied and that the wishes of the hon. member should be carried out. I have since heard no complaints. The fact that the hon. member has brought the matter to my attention will also bring it to the

attention of the people, and if there is any difficulty, I shall be glad to see that the hon. member's wishes are carried out.
I notice an item of $800 for a fire-inspector. What does this inspector do?

This fire inspector receives only $800 from the department, but he is also an employee of the Interior Department. Parliament passed an Act giving the Railway Commission powers in regard to fire protection along the lines of railway so that the commission has power to issue an order as to what a railway must do in that regard. This man has been appointed chief fire inspector.
While the commission does not control the railway companies it has power to order certain things to be done by the management of those railways.

By the railway companies themselves. The commission may order the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern or any other railway that comes under its jurisdiction to do certain things towards fire protection along their line of railway.
But the commission cannot give such orders to the Government railways?
No, because the Government railway system is not under the Railway Commission in any way and never has been.

Some months ago the Board of Railway Commissioners made an order for a union station at Toronto. Can the minister tell us what progress is being made with that station? I admit that it is a little difficult at the present time to get money for the purpose, but this is a joint station in which more than one railway is interested. If ever there was a place where strangers risk their lives in getting on or off trains, it is in Toronto. My hon. friend from North York (Mr. Armstrong) knows his way about the Toronto station and he does not get lost; but if I were to hand in my bill to the railway companies for taking strangers in and out of that building, 1 would have a comfortable living for the rest of my life. You may be standing right beside a train wondering how you are going to get through it to your train and suddenly it will move away. Perhaps the next time a trainman will break a train up in two sections four or

five cars down At other times you vill have to climb in between cars in order to get to your own train. I c in readily understand the difficulty at the present time of hurrying on the matter, but it has been announced during the past few months that work has been proceeding on this new station. Can the minister tell us what the companies are doing or how far they have advanced towards carrying out the order of the Board of Railway Commissioners?

There has been a delay for a long time in regard to the Toronto railway terminal question. There is no place in Canada where a proper station and adequate terminal facilities are required so much as right in Toronto. Trouble arose over the plans, the cost, and so on, and after a great deal of delay, the matter was finally agreed on by all concerned. I have been urging for a long time that the railway companies should come to some arrangement because we wanted to build an examining warehouse and customs office adjoining that property and we could not start with it because the railways could not get their plans right. However, their plans were approved last fall, and perhaps the hon. member will remember-it was announced in the press-that Mr. Leonard was appointed manager of the terminal company formed to construct that station. I know that the contract has been awarded to Peter Lyall and Sons, Limited, and they have instructions, as I am informed, to proceed with the work and to carry it through to completion as quickly as possible. As the plans have been definitely settled, we can now go on with our work. Probably there will be no difficulty in the future about the station at Toronto. The investigation that we are likely to have into the railway systems of Canada will give good results in regard to stations of that kind. In our large cities there are terminals which not only are an inconvenience to the public but mean an unnecessary expenditure of money, and it seems to me that the terminals in such centres should be all in one place. In Montreal, the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk, and the Canadian Northern have their own terminals and they are all spending a great deal of money on terminal facilities. At another session, we shall have a report in regard to such matters and it will be of great advantage to the public in the future.
I can assure the hon. member that the contract has been let for the Toronto station and the railway companies have in-

formed me that they will push forward the work as fast as possible.

Has the Grand Trunk
Railway Company made any claim on the Government to assist them in defraying the expense of such reconstruction as they have undertaken of their station in Montreal?
No application has been received, so far as I know.

For a good many years
there was an arbitration board to settle certain difficulties between the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial. It seemed to be almost a perpetual board. I think that it lasted so long that one or two of its members died before a report wa3 made. Is that board doing anything now? Are these vacancies filled?
No, it died a natural death.

The difficulties were
straightened out?

All straightened out; no
difficulties at all remain.

I am afraid there are
still difficulties. Reverting to the station at Montreal: the situation there is something like that at Toronto and it has not been modified by the recent fire. I think the Board of Railway Commissioners had the matter of elevating the tracks in Montreal under consideration. Did they give an order about the Montreal station at one time?

They have investigated,
but nothing has been settled.

The entrance of the
Grand Trunk to Montreal is on the level while the Canadian Pacific railway is on the hill and the Canadian Northern under the hill-constituting three distinct kinds of entrance. It may be difficult at this stage to overcome all the difficulties that arise in the way of making ideal accommodation in Montreal for passenger traffic, but, for the convenience of the public it would be much better if, in this, as well as in other large centres, the railway passenger terminals could be concentrated. People getting off the steamer at Montreal go to the Canadian Pacific railway expecting to go right through to their destination. I have seen them, when they showed their tickets, told that they were in the wrong station and that they must go to the Grand Trunk. Of course it is only two blocks away, but when those people got to the Grand Trunk
probably they found that the train -had gone and they would have to wait over until the next day. Of course, it will be difficult and expensive to concentrate the passenger business in such a great centre as Montreal, but it will be a great advantage to the travelling public. I will go further and say, it would be a great convenience to the travelling public if some arrangement could be made by which tickets would be made interchangeable over the different roads.
That is what I advocated.

I think' it could be
brought about. Of course, when you approach the companies about these things you are told that there are insurmountable difficulties. But tickets are issued on the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific railway that are honoured when you get to some other line. To make tickets interchangeable might cause some inconvenience, but I do not see why it should be impossible to so arrange that a man w'ho has paid his money to the Canadian Pacific for a ticket should be able to present that ticket on a Grand Trunk train and the Grand Trunk get their pay from the Canadian Pacific. Can the minister tell me if the Railway Commission was asked to approve of the rebuilding of the Grand Trunk station at Montreal?

I have made no inquiries
and there is no information in the department on the subject. I see by the newspapers that the Grand Trunk are building a temporary station. I will inquire as to the point the hon. gentleman raises.

As I recollect it, within
the last three or four months, the city of Montreal and the Grand Trunk got together and went before the Railway Board with a view to having the work gone on with. The Railway Board, while admitting the need for the work, thought it inopportune to issue an order on the subject on account of the difficulty of raising money at this time to carry on works of this kind. This subject of passenger stations is an old-standing grievance in Montreal. I recollect reporting the proceedings in the city hall of Montreal 25 years ago or more when this very subject was under discussion. The late Sir Joseph Hickson, general manager of the Grand Trunk, had a plan for raising the tracks of the Grand Trunk and building a new station. This question really takes us back thirty years or more, and things are in the same position as they

were then, except that lately the Bonaven-ture station was burned down-through no fault of the Grand Trunk Company-and we now have a very primitive station indeed. I suppose it cannot be otherwise under the circumstances. But I hope that something will be done before the new station is built. As the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said, there is great inconvenience in Montreal by reason of the many railway passenger stations in the city. We have the Grand Trunk station, the Windsor station of the Canadian Pacific, and now we are to have the Canadian Northern tunnel station at Dorchester street. The traveller at Montreal is bewildered by the number of railway stations. I have heard the suggestion made that an arrangement should be come to by which the Grand Trunk passenger trains might run on the upper level and the passenger business be concentrated at the Windsor station, the tracks on the lower level to be used for freight business. I do not know whether there is anything in that or not. But if the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk could be brought together in the Windsor station, then, with the Canadian Northern on the other side of the square opposite St. James' cathedral, there would be fairly close concentration, and the whole would be a great improvement. There is another station, the Viger Square station, which is mainly used for traffic going to Quebec, while the western traffic generally leaves by the Windsor station. But the old idea in Montreal was to have one central station. When the Canadian Pacific railway was first started, the city of Montreal voted $1,000,000 for a station at Viger square, then considered to be in the eastern part of the city, but, some time after that a company was formed under which the railway obtained permission to build the Windsor station, and there the western traffic has been concentrated. The minister will be entitled to the gratitude of the city of Montreal if he can bring this condition of affairs to an end. If the Grand Trunk is allowed to put up a very expensive station and to raise their tracks, then the idea of having a union station in Montreal will have to be abandoned for two or three generations at least. Whatever is decided should be gone on with. Montreal has already a large population-over six hundred thousand-and when the war is over and matters fairly settled, within a few years [Mr. Marcil.l
thereafter we count on a million people in Montreal. This railway business is very urgent, and if anything can be done to improve matters it should be done soon.

I quite agree with the hon.
member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and have stated similar views. In arranging for terminals at Montreal there are not only three but four railways to be considered, the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific, and the Canadian Northern. If it is possible to bring them together in one station, that should be done. The Grand Trunk now have only a temporary station, their station having been burned down.
I understand that the reason they have gone on with this work is that it will take at least $15,000,000 to make the terminals at Montreal and to elevate the tracks. That has not been done. It should be done if there is any possibility of the railways being brought together as suggested by the hon. member. Under present conditions there is, I believe, no possible chance that the Grand Trunk will proceed with any work of that kind during the coming summer. It is the intention to have an investigation made as to the railway situation, and I am strongly of the opinion that there should be some way of compelling the railways to join their passenger terminals together at these large centres of population, [DOT]on the lines suggested by the hon. member. I do not think there is any possibility of much being done during the next few months in any of the large centres, and I am in hopes that when the next session opens we shall have a report that will place every hon. member of the House in a position to judge as to the proper method of dealing with the railway systems in Canada; and the question of terminals is of course, one of the most important features of the whole railway situation. I therefore think we can safely allow the matter to rest until the opening of the next session, and I hope that an arrangement, or perhaps some legislation', may be procured which will put the Board of Railway Commissioners in a position to deal with the question in a place, like Montreal, where the providing of proper terminals facilities would be in the public interest as well as in the interest of the different railways. The saving would, of course, be very great.

I suggest to the minister that he should impress on the railways the

necessity of providing in the present union station at Toronto an information bureau in a conspicuous place, or at least constables with distinctive caps, so that passengers coming off one train and desiring to take another train, may obtain information. It is almost impossible for a person to get information at the union station in Toronto and, as has been said, there is probably no place on earth where people are more likely to become bewildered. I have seen people hunting all over the place for some man from whom they could get information. I have asked about trains and *have received very curt answers, so much so that I have felt almost like taking the fellow by the coat collar and shaking his head a bit.
What size is he?

It does not matter to me about the size, they all look alike to me. I want them to be civil. They are not very civil, and do not put themselves out of the way, especially for women and children. If the minister has any control over matters of that kind, I wish he would see that the three railways make 6ome such provision as I have suggested.

I agree that it is necessary in a station to have a good information bureau. There is one upstairs at Toronto now, but of course there should be one downstairs as well. I will take the matter up with the railway companies and endeavour to have them provide a place of that kind. There is a room in the Union station which, I think, would make a splendid information 'bureau, and we may be able to get it as we shall probably have prohibition in force by September. I will aak the railway company if they cannot make-
That booze joint.
-into an information bureau.
I think the members have a grievance against the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway for not running the Grand Trunk sleeping car between Ottawa and Brockville during this session.
Has that car not been on? I wish it had been brought to our attention 'before.

It has not been on this session. The Canadian Pacific Railway have also neglected to put on the sleeper
that, during other sessions, lay at Broad street station at night, so that members might board the car after the House rose and awake in Montreal. That was a very great convenience.

I do not think there should be any difficulty about the car from Ottawa to Brockville, as in discussing with the Grand Trunk officials the question of Pullman traffic in Canada, not long before Parliament met, the question of this car was taken up, and it is certainly a great surprise to me to learn that it has not been operated.

Then in other years we had a chair car from Brockville to Ottawa over the Canadian Pacific railway. That car has been taken off on week days; it runs now only on Sundays. That causes great inconvenience to travellers. A man has to be at the station before train time if he desires to get a seat.
If he has his wife or children with him he has to go down to the station at least half an hour before the train is due to leave to get a seat, because the only first class coach is usually filled. It does inconvenience the travelling public a good deal. When a chair car is on the intending passengers go down on time and get their seats. I wish to bring another mattter to the attention of my hon. friend. At Iroquois one of the soldiers doing duty on the canal there was killed in November last.
He was drowned, was he not?

No. This soldier's name was Barbour, and he went to assist the lockmaster, and the crank flew around and struck him and killed him. He leaves a widow-I do not know if there are any children-who is not in very good circumstances. Application was made, 1 believe, to the Railway Department, or to the Militia Department, and they declined to do anything on the ground that, legally speaking, they were not liable, which was undoubtedly correct. I suppose that as a matter of law the soldier had no business to turn that crank, and he was negligent in interfering with the work of the look-master. But he was there for the time being, assisting in putting some boats through, being glad, I suppose, to have something to do to keep him busy, and this well intended effort resulted in his death. I am not appealing to the minister on the ground of any legal right that the widow has, but I do appeal to his sympathy, and suggest

that he look into this matter and see whether or not a compassionate allowance cannot be given to this widow, who requires assistance very much at the present time.
I do not claim that the widow has any legal right, but the circumstances are such that I think the Government might well consider the case.

This is the first I have heard of the case, and I will he very glad to look into it. I do not think it would be possible, even if we so decided, to make a compassionate allowance during the present session. The man may be said to have been on active service, and I wondered whether an application had been made to the Militia Department for a pension. That is a matter which might be considered in a case of this kind, and I believe the Militia Department have been very liberal in such cases when men were on active service. I will take the matter up with the Militia Department. If the widow is entitled to a pension under the Militia Act, it would be much better for her than a compassionate allowance.
Mr. .GRAHAM:	It would be more permanent.

Yes. I do not think that
the payment of a certain amount would be of the same benefit; even the interest probably would not amount to so much as the pension. I will look into the case, but I would suggest in the meantime that if the family have taken no action with the Militia Department they should make an application so that it may go before the Pension Board.

I doubt whether the
widow would have any claim to a pension; her husband was not killed in the performance of his duty.

He was killed at the locks
while assisting the lock-master, and that circumstance might be considered. At any-rate I think it would be well to have the case considered first by the Militia Department. If that has already been done, I will get the report, and if they cannot do anything, I will see that the matter is taken up by the Railway Department with the view of considering whether something should be done to assist the family. '

I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in going into details, or in discussing the abstract principles on which our railway systems are conducted; but throughout the different time tables one can find many instances

showing that it is the desire of each railway company to run its own business without regard to the passengers who are carried on other railways. They do not care about the connections made from other roads than their own. There are oases in the time-tables where, say, a train leaves a junction point at 10 o'clock, and another train crosses that point say at two minutes after 10 o'clock. There is no chance of the train at the junction point waiting the two minutes to allow a connection to be made by the other train. The time tables are filled with cases of that kind, and disappointments are numerous because of the lack of some consideration being shown to the travelling public.
Mr. MARCH.: They do not co-operate in the interests of the public.

Not at all. The railways are run for the railway companies and not for the public convenience. To illustrate, I went to Toronto on one occasion last winter, having made an appointment at Woodstock, in the constituency of my hon. friend from Oxford. I travelled on a Canadian Northern train from Ottawa and it reached Toronto five minutes behind time, and I missed the Canadian Pacific railway train for Woodstock. I made inquiries as to when I could go on to Woodstock and was told that I could not go until night unless I went by Stratford. I commented on the situation to a gold-topped man, such as the hon. gentleman spoke of, and he was very discourteous about it. I told him that he was not there for the purpose of being discourteous, and he said that the Canadian Northern railway did not count. There were several members of Parliament there, of whom the Chairman of the Railway Committee was one, and the hon. member from North Grey another. The official told the latter that he would have to wait until night before he could leave Toronto, although he desired to get home on the Saturday to attend to his business. I took exception to the statement of the official that the Canadian Northern railway did not count, but he was so big that he scared me off, and I let it go at that. Later on he sent through another member of Parliament an expression of regret for the language he had used. I was forced with another member to go to Shakespeare on the Grand Trunk and to engage a motor car to come from Woodstock, 20 miles distant, to take us there to fulfil an appointment at one o'clock in the afternoon. I

would like to impress upon the committee the fact that experiences of that kind are more general than may be supposed. A communication should he sent from this Parliament to the Board of Railway Commissioners, whose duty, I apprehend it is, to take hold of these questions, to study the time-tables and correct such abuses so that the public may have the benefits, for the securing of which, public money has gone to these big corporations.

While we are ventilating grievances, may I take the acting minister down East with me for a moment? I would like to call his attention to the advantage of the through passenger services given on the Intercolonial railway between Montreal and Halifax by means of the Ocean Limited and the Maritime Express. I do not wish to criticise the action of the minister, or of the department, in taking away the service of the Ocean Limited when the traffic does not permit the running of more than one of these trains. But I do want to call his attention to the fact that if we cannot have both of these services, and if one of them must be taken away, in the public interest, in the interest especially of through passenger traffic, and in the interest of the Tailway itself, the Ocean Limited should be kept on and the Maritime Express taken off. All along the railway we have local express services which are sufficient, generally speaking, for the local traffic. I will explain the difference between the through service of the Ocean Limited and of the Maritime Express. If you leave the Maritime Provinces, or northern New Brunswick, by the Maritime Express, in the middle of the night, getting into Moncton at nine or ten o'clock, and Newcastle and Bathurst about twelve or one o'clock, you are on the train all day again and only reach Montreal at six or seven o'clock in the evening if you are on time. Then, it is too late for any person to attend to any business in Montreal. He has to spend all next day and wait until the morning after before he can return East. If a man leaves Moncton, or the north shore of New Brunswick, by the Ocean Limited early in the evening he reaches Montreal at eight o'clock next morning; if he is a business man he has the whole day in Montreal to attend to his business and he can take the train again at 7.30 in the evening and reach home next morning or early in the day, whereas, by the other train, he has to wait until next morning and only reaches
northern New Brunswick next day, and St. John late in the afternoon. The minister will understand the great difference it makes to the travelling public. Then take the southern portion of New Brunswick, St. John and the neighbourhood; by taking away the Ocean Limited you ignore totally the traffic between Montreal and St. John. The Ocean Limited, when it is running, leaves Montreal in the evening about the same time that the Canadian Pacific leaves Montreal for St. John and the man who travels on the Ocean Limited reaches St. John next day about the same time a6 the man who travels on the Canadian Pacific. Therefore, there is an inducement for people to take advantage of the Government railway instead of the Canadian Pacific. If you take off the Ocean Limited for a considerable, or even for a short time, the travelling public from the southern part of New Brunswick have to take the Canadian Pacific and once they become used to that road they continue to patronize it even after the Ocean Limited is put on again. The Ocean Limited therefore loses the traffic for the whole year round. If the local services on the Intercolonial railway are not sufficient to meet the demands, it might be to the advantage of the Government railway to augment that service in one section or another, and then if only one of these through trains can be retained, I maintain that in the interest of the road and of the travelling public, it should be the Ocean Limited and not the Maritime Express. I hope my suggestion will commend itself to the favourable consideration of the minister. I know that I voice the general feeling of the public in the Maritime Provinces
Mr. RiEID: The Ocean Limited is taken off for a few months during the winter for the 6ame reason as that which applies to trains taken off during winter by other railway companies.
I am only speaking of taking off one train.

I understand that. The reason that the Maritime Express is left on is that you may have a train leaving Montreal in the morning if you are going through to Halifax. The Canadian Pacific has a night train leaving Montreal. If we were to leave on the Ocean Limited you would have two trains leaving Montreal at night and going through to the Maritime Provinces and you would have

none in the morning. Passengers from the West arriving in Montreal at 9 or 10 in the evening, or at 7 in the morning on the Grand Trunk, Canadian Northern, or Canadian Pacific, would have to wait until 7 or 7.30 o'clock at night before they could proceed on their journey through to St. John or Halifax. The object of having two trains, one in the morning, the Maritime Express, owned by the Government Railway system, and one in the evening, owned by the Canadian Pacific system, is that the travelling public may have an opportunity of leaving Montreal for the lower provinces twice a day instead of once as would be the' result if you had a train running on the Ocean Limited time. The only way to satisfy the hon. member would be to keep the Ocean Limited on.

If the department could by any possibility keep on the double service the year round that is what we would like. Taking everything into consideration, I believe it would be more to the general advantage to keep the Ocean Limited on, if only one train is kept on. I perceive the advantage of being able to make connections with trains from the West, but on several occasions when I have come from the West it has been my luck to reach Montreal just in time to miss the Maritime Express, so that even if that train had not been on I would have been just as well off. On the other hand, other trains are supposed to arrive in Montreal in the evening, and these people have the advantage of making a connection with the Ocean Limited; so that, taking everything into consideration, as far as connection from' the West is concerned, I do not think it makes much difference. It does make a great difference to the people of the Maritime Provinces, and more particularly to the people travelling between Montreal and St. John. If the people are without the through service on the Government railway for three or four months in the year they will do without it for the other seven or eight months, and thus a great deal of [DOT]traffic is diverted from the Intercolonial to the Canadian Pacific that would not be diverted if the Ocean Limited were kept on.

I cannot agree with the hon. member that the connection at Montreal with the Maritime Express from .the West, New York, and other places is not a very important one. I have arrived at Montreal on the Grand Trunk many times, and I

think that on the whole the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific trains arrive at Montreal pretty nearly always on time. There is some little difference between the arrival of the trains from the West, New York, and other places and the departure of the trains for the East, and as a rule, connections are pretty well made.
I do not think the public would stand for the two trains leaving Montreal at practically the same hour at night, and having no train in the morning. We think that we should always have a morning train from Montreal for the lower provinces. With regard to keeping the Ocean Limited on throughout the year, it has always been the policy to run it for a certain number of months only, and take it off in the winter. As an experiment the present Minister of Railways allowed the Ocean Limited to run for the whole twelve months two or three years ago, but the traffic was so small that there was a very, very heavy loss. The hon. member knows that it costs $800 to run the train from Montreal right through, and $800 coming back again,- or $1,600 a day. The loss was so great that the minister had to go back to the system that prevailed before he took office. I could not say whether the traffic now would justify the Ocean Limited being kept on for the whole twelve months. However, it will be on again in the next few days, and will of course continue, even under the old. arrangement, until next fall. On the minister's return I shall draw his attention to my hon. friend's suggestion, and also take it up with the general manager with a view to seeing whether it would be advisable to give the experiment another trial. I agree that the more trains you have the more convenient it is for the public. But, of course, regard must be had to the public interests, when a train is being run at a heavy loss. I am very glad the hon. member has brought the matter up.

I was not criticising
the taking off of the Ocean Limited during a certain period of the year. I admit that it might not be in the interest of the department to have the two trains running in the winter months, and of the two I would prefer to have the Ocean Limited kept on. Another suggestion I would make is that it might be better to have a local train from Montreal to points east in Quebec rather than run the entire train through from Montreal to Halifax or St. John.
i

I endorse
what the hon. gentleman has said. The Ocean Limited would give very much better accommodation to the people in Nova Scotia than the Maritime Express. A man going by the Maritime Express to Sydney-and the bulk of the traffic is east of Truro-has to ivait seven or eight hours at Truro before he can get a train to take him to his destination; whereas if he went by the Ocean Limited, he would have to wait only two or three hours, as he would be able to make connection with the train from Halifax. If, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Gloucester, the Ocean Limited were continued instead of the Maritime Express and a local train were put on between Montreal and points east in Quebec, the whole country would be very much better served, because much better time would be made. Is the minister in a position to give me the information I wrote him about a couple of days ago, with respect to the Antigonish flower garden.

I wired for that, but I am
sorry it has not yet come to hand. I will wire again to-day, saying I must have the information by to-morrow.

As the minister has explained it does not pay at a certain time of the year to run both the Maritime Express and the Ocean Limited. If from a business point of view only one train can be kept on, I would prefer to have the Ocean Limited. However, the explanation given by the minister seems reasonable, and it might be more in the interests of the railway and of the people in a certain section of the country to have the
4	p.m. express kept on. Another thing I should like to point out to the minister, and about which I have spoken to the general manager several times, is that the Maritime Express leaves Montreal too early in the, morning for people coming from the West, except those from Toronto. People travelling on the Canadian Pacific Railway train from Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury or Winnipeg, arriving in Montreal about nine o'clock in the morning, miss the Maritime Express, which leaves at 8.15 and have then to spend a whole day in. Montreal. I would suggest that when the Ocean Limited is taken off, the Maritime Express should leave Montreal about twelve o'clock, as it did some years ago. This would give passengers from the West a chance to get home to points between Levis and Moncton without having to wait twentvfour hours in Montreal. Under the present schedule they have to stay in Montreal from 9 or 9.30 in the morning until 8.15 the next morning, which is very inconvenient. I would suggest that the express start about eleven or twelve o'clock, but twelve would be better, as it would give business men in Ottawa a chance to catch the train. I think this change would be to the advantage, not only of the Intercolonial, but of the whole travelling public between Levis and Moncton. When the Ocean Limited is taken off I think a good many passengers will take the Canadian Pacific railway for points East unless the time of the departure of the Maritime Express is changed, as they would not want to stay in Montreal a whole day. This causes the Intercolonial to lose a great many passengers going to the Maritime Provinces. The making of the change in the way I propose would keep our passengers and would be to the interest of the Intercolonial.
I would like to make another suggestion in regard to a change in the administration. 1 have already complained several tunes that the division between Montmagny and Campbellton is under the control of New Brunswick officials. I would suggest that instead of that, the whole line in Quebec, from Montreal to Campbellton, should lie put under the direction of the Superintendent of Railways. '[DOT] hat would divide more equally the work of the two inspectors, as the one who has charge from Montmagny to Campbellton has under his direction several small branches, such as the Fredericton branch, so lhat he has a good deal more mileage 11 administer than the Superintendent of Railways. My suggestion, if canied out, wouid be satisfactory to ;he people of the province of Quebec; it would settle all the difficulties that we have had for years with the officials at Campb.iikon and ii would also be of great advantage to the administration of the road. The officials at Campbellton who administer the Montmagny-Campbellton division do not know anything about that road; they are all strangers to us; they do not know the giades except from what they see on the plans; and they are liable to make many mistakes. It often happens that trains are delayed on sidings just on that account. If the people appointed to look after that division were men from the province of Quebec who knew the ground, they could do their work more efficiently. I make this suggestion in the interest of the road and also of the people of the province of Quebec, and it would at once remove all the friction



arising between the employees on the two divisions. All the employees in the Camp-bellton office who run the trains on our division speak nothing but English and belong to New Brunswick, and our people in the province of Quebec do not like to be run by those strangers. We prefer to be under the control of our own men whom we know, and it would make conditions a great deal better than they are now.

The hon. member mentioned this matter to me a few days ago, and I think the suggestion is worthy of consideration. I am taking it up with the management now, and I shall be glad to see that every consideration is given to his suggestion.

I would just like to add one word about what the hon. member for North Perth (Mt. Morphy) says about trains not waiting for passengers from other trains. I believe that no people are so badly used in that regard as are the people of Dufferin and North Grey. There is a daily train from Toronto.to Owen Sound, a distance of about 120 miles, and from Owen Sound to Meaford on the east is 20 miles. To get across that 20 miles you have to go about 240 miles from Owen Sound to Toronto and back to Meaford. If the trains would wait at Inglewood, about 60 miles would be cut off, and you could reach your destination in about five hours, whereas if you leave Shelburne or Owen Sound in the morning, you arrive at Inglewood about eight in the morning and have to wait until six at night. One train is the Grand Trunk and the otheT is the Canadian Pacific, and there is only about four minutes difference in the time. Many people have been trying to get the matter arranged with the Board of Railway Commissioners, so that the trains might be compelled to wait for each other. I think it is up to the Government to see that something is done in a case like that. No matter whether you go from north to south, or from south to north, you have a ten hours' wait.
I would like to make a suggestion to the Government in regard to the taking away of agents at night on the line between Owen Sound and Toronto. Up to a few months ago the agents used to wait at their offices until the last train, which arrives at Owen Sound between ten and eleven, was-in. For the last few months at many of the stations the agents have been taken away at night, and baggage for one of these stations is thrown off on the platform without any one to look after it, or it goes on

to Owen Sound and it is sent back the next day. That is very unfair, because the line is a paying one; in fact, I have heard it said that there is no better paying line in Canada than the one between Owen Sound and Toronto.

Such matters should be and can be settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners. There was a similar case at the town of Brockville, where one train left a minute or two before another one arrived. We had the matter arranged by applying to the Board of Railway Commissioners. Their officials look into the matter, and if they find any injustice, they issue an order which the Tailway company must carry out. If the hon. member will give me a written statement of any complaints he has to make, I shall be very glad to bring them before the Board of Railway Commissioners, or the parties interested can do so themselves. All they have to do is to lay their complaint before the Board and ask for a hearing, which the Board are compelled to give, and, as a rule, the decisions of the Board have been satisfactory. The hon. member can either adopt that method of procedure or, if he wishes me to deal with the matter, I shall be glad to take it up with the Board.

I spoke of this matter a few minutes ago, and I rise for the purpose of putting another point of view before the Acting Minister of Railways. People do not like to complain; they do not organize to go to the Board of Railway Commissioners, because a solicitor has frequently to be employed, and that costs money; and, while no doubt they get every consideration when they do go before the Board, I think this is a case where the Government should take action by communicating to the Railway Commission the fact, that this abuse exists throughout the whole railway system. The trouble is caused by each railway acting on the principle of carrying on its work without any consideration to any other railway, to the absolute disadvantage of the public. It is a shame that such should be the case, and the abuse should be corrected. If the hon. minister would state, so that his statement will appear on Hansard, that it is the desire of the Government that the Board of Railway Commissioners should take up this question and see what is the true state of affairs, with a view to correcting the abuse themselves, without the people making com-

plaint, a great benefit would accrue to the people of this country.

I will bring this matter to
the attention of the Railway Commission as suggested by the hon. member. Complaints are sometimes made against the railways for which little grounds are found to exist when they are looked into; but there are undoubtedly grievances. In a specific ease such as that mentioned by the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) there is no reason why the matter should not be investigated at once. We had a great deal, of trouble with the connection at Brock-ville, but we got that straightened out.

I would not have spoken on the subject at the present time but that the judges took it up, and the very timetable itself showed that there was only three or four minutes' difference in the time of the arrival of the trains at the crossing, and the losing of the train at that point might mean a hundred miles of travel for a passenger, or the loss of a day. Not only did the time-table show that one train, would have only a few minutes to wait for the other, but it was also shown that at the other end of the line the Grand Trunk train had ample time to wait. We could get no redress.

The Act provides that complaints of grievance can be made to the board not only by interested parties but by the Minister of Railways, or the board of its own volition can issue an order on a matter in which no complaint has been made. There is plenty of room to have the board act in this matter.

I desire the minister to get my point of view, especially in view of one part of his remarks. He said that if any member wishes to make a complaint to the Railway Commission the matter will be dealt with. I think members of Parliament have their time pretty well taken up with the miscellaneous duties they have to perform, and I am under the impression that the Railway Commission is there for the public benefit and to correct these difficulties the moment they hear of them. The reason I spoke was-and I have no doubt the same is true of other hon. members-that I assume the commissioners will read this in Hansard and learn that there is a great public complaint which has not reached them. Having sovereign powers, as you might say, and an equally sovereign duty I 216i
to the people of this country, if they feel there is an abuse they should correct it without waiting for a member- of Parliament to call it to their attention.

I desire to add a word
with regard to the situation, in Montreal, in the hope that it will reach the Railway Commission or this new commission, to which reference has been made. I said a few words about the desirability of concentrating the passenger terminals at Dominion square, by inducing the Grand Trunk to link up with the Canadian Pacific and use the Windsor station. With the Canadian Northern on the other side of the square we would have the three railways close together. Another great grievance in Montreal is that of street crossings. On one line they have adopted one system and on another a different system. The Grand Trunk uses the old gate system, and one may approach the railway track when he is in a hurry only to find that the gate is shut and there is no means of knowing whether he is to be kept for a minute or for half an hour before he is allowed to cross. He can take the risk of trying to cross, and he may be crushed, as a great many people have been crushed, under the train. The Canadian Pacific Railway system has been to close up the streets entirely. Under the Canadian Pacific track running from Windsor station, Decarie avenue is the only crossing that is open for many blocks. This is in Notre Dame da Grace, an extension of Montreal, which has progressed more rapidly than any other part Of the city and is now quite densely populated. It is crossed by the line of the Canadian Pacific, and one finds that between Decarie avenue and Montreal West for a distance of fifteen or twenty blocks, every street is closed. The children going to school, the people going to church, the people on their way between Sherbrooke street and the Lower Lachine road may have to walk a mile or a mile and a half out of their way to find a subway which allows them to pass under the Canadian Pacific track. I suppose the company have the power to do this, because the road was built before this part of the city was developed and the crossings that were closed were only farm crossings. But the fact that the company had the right, does not make the situation any less a burden on the people, and I think that means of relief should be found. I hardly know which is worse, the level crossing .system of the Grand Trunk with its gates which

you can got through at some time in the day, or the system of the Canadian Pacific railway which prevents you from getting through at all except by going a roundabout way. The railway companies protect themselves; and of course nobody would wish to see the railways of Canada go behind in any way, but it seems to me there should be some supervising authority to look after the interests of the people. Some years ago I had the advantage of travelling in France, and there I found such a thing as a level crossing to be very rare; the same is true of England. The railways run eitheT over or under the roads. But the rights of the public seem to have been protected; there is something left for the common citizen; he can cross the street without danger of being run over and without being compelled to go half a dozen blocks out of his way. To .solve the very complicated problem in Montreal, these several -matters should be called to the attention of the Railway Board or of the new commission.

I shall be glad to act on the suggestion of the hon. member and call attention of the Railway Commission to the matter. It is a big question and one that will bear examination by the new commission, and I hope that great results will follow that examination.

I had not the opportunity of saying anything with respect to Intercolonial affairs when the Estimates were going through, but I understand that the privilege is still open for members to call attention to matters which they deem of importance with regard to that system. I wish to refer to what has been stated by the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best). I did net hear the whole of his remarks, but I understand the gist of them to be that there is no proper connection made between the different systems of railways, no regulation or understanding by which one train waits for another. He spoke especially of one case in Ontario, but so far as we are concerned in Eastern Canada that is not the case. The feelings of two sets of passengers in trains of this kind are very different. The train load that is held up is swearing at the delay, while the passenger who wishes to take that train is hoping that the train will wait. There is a very strong conflict of opinion about a situation of that kind, and differences are not always easily reconcilable. I have frequently had to wait at Truro from

8 o'clock in the evening until 11.30 o'clock for the arrival of the Canadian Pacific Railway train. I would have arrived at Truro about the middle of the day and would have waited there until the Halifax train came in at 8 o'clock, when, in the ordinary course of events, I could have proceeded towards my home in Cape Breton; but we have been frequently held up until nearly midnight waiting for the arrival of the Canadian Pacific Railway train. If courtesy as between railways is scarce in Ontario, it is carried to the extreme at our end of the Dominion, and we should like to have matters adjusted so that the long stoppages at our end would be curtailed and part of them applied to Ontario. That would be an evening up that would be satisfactory all round. Only two or three days ago I waited for an hour and a half at Truro for a train. Coming from Cape Breton we were delayed for four hours 'by a little obstacle, a little worse than a cow crossing the track, at Tracadie. We lost our connection at Truro and had to wait for a whole day. This may be nobody's fault and accidents .of that kind will happen; but it is very annoying. For the last six weeks or two months the arrival of trains at Sydney and adjacent points has been far from satisfactory. Sometimes the train from Halifax, only two or three hundred miles away, is 10 hours late. That is most extraordinary, and we cannot find out exactly what causes the trouble. I used to say, speaking facetiously, that when we had a manager with a salary o-f $5,000 or $6,000 a year, we had regular trains; but as the salary increased the time became worse, and if this manager received $30,000 we would have no trains at all. I would bring the size of the salary and the lateness of the trains to the serious consideration of the minister.
I wish to bring seriously to the attention of the minister the lack of proper facilities for the handling of traffic at North Sydney, which is really the eastern Atlantic terminus of the Intercolonial. Of course there is a terminus at Sydney, but there is very little business done there. The main business is done at the terminus at North Sydney, where connection is made for the island of Newfoundland. It may interest the minister to know that until 19 years ago we had not water terminus at North Sydney, and no business was done at that point in connection with the Intercolonial. But in 1897 a wharf was built and the road was run down to the water. At that time there was practically no business between

the island of Newfoundland and the Intercolonial railway, but that business has since grown by leaps and bounds so that now, during open navigation, which is about 10 months of the year, we ship outwards on the Intercolonial about 10 cars a day, sometimes 15 cars a day of freight going over the Intercolonial and on the boats to Newfoundland. When I was in North Sydney the other day, there were about 100 cars standing on the sidings, both down at the wharf and up at the station, waiting for boats to carry the freight to Newfoundland. With the in-coming business I am not so familiar. I am sure that the passenger business from Newfoundland must be a very material source of income for the Intercolonial, while the handling of freight, such as fish from Newfoundland, must be profitable. The business handled at this point is enormous, but the facilities are absolutely inadequate. The wharf is too small. It is not long enough and is not wide enough, and is in no sense commensurate with the business to be handled there. I would ask the acting minister to bring this to the notice of the real Minister of Railways-although if reports be true I am talking to the right man now. There are two, and sometimes three, boats on the Newfoundland route. There is only proper room for one boat at the wharf. The boats trading along the coast that want to land fish and other freight at North Sydney are compelled to tie up at some other wharf and cart their freight back to the railway. This is far from being just to	our people, because they	oughtto have room to	bring	their
vessels alongside the railway and be enabled to put their freight aboard the cars with the least possible expense and trouble. But there is always a Newfoundland boat there, as the service is a daily one. There is land near the wharf that the minister could buy at a reasonable price for the purpose of extending the wharf.
Then, the station at North Sydney is far from being sufficient. About half a mile from the station there ie a little Indian village. I am far from casting any slurs upon Indians or upon poor Indian women, but it is a fact that white people do not care to be obliged to congregate with them at railway stations and in small railway rooms. We have only the one room there, a small room for a large passenger traffic. Passengers are compelled to wait in that room all huddled together, all kinds of people. It is quite proper that the Indian
women and the Indians should have some shelter, but I think it would be well that the accommodation for passengers should be large enough to obviate the crowding of other people in with them as is the case with the present email station at North Sydney. Even apart from any objection of that kind, the station is far from what it should be. It was built 25 years ago when traffic was small and the town of North Sydney and surrounding places were not as large as they are now. There was no provision for Newfoundland traffic at that time, and so the station to-day is far from what it ought to be. I submit to the minister that when he undertakes to enlarge the wharf, which must be done in order to handle the business, he should also give some attention to the enlargement of the railway station.
I wish to bring'up also another matter in connection with the handling of trains in that vicinity. The minister may tell me that I should go to the general manager with the case, but the manager is not available to us; we cannot see him, and, as was well said by the hon. member for Westmoreland ((Mr. Copp), while this road remains a Government iroad, this Parliament, and this Government, and the Minister of Railways cannot divest themselves of responsibility. Members of Parliament will properly go to the minister with their complaints and requests and will expect them to be transmitted to the manager and his staff to have them attended to. The minister is awaTe that the town, from which I come, and the immediate vicinity are pretty well populated. We have a series of villages or towns along the first ten miles of the road from North Sydney. There is in the vicinity a large quarry operated by the Dominion Steel Company, and next to that are the Colonial Coal Company's works, the town of Florence, and the town of Sydney; so that for the first ten miles, there is practically a continuous community. The people there take advantage in the evenings to travel into North Sydney by the train from Halifax, which passes about 7 o'clock, returning by a train which goes out at 9 o'clock. Thus the people can go into Sydney and get back to their homes that night. That is all right, but on Saturday night, which is the night of all nights that the people want to go to town, there is no outgoing train; that is, no train leaves Sydney on Saturday night. If the people in the district go into town by the 7 o'clock train, they cannot get home

unless they drive, which means that they are realty prohibited from getting into town.
Is the train which leaves Sydney at 9 o'clock the through train going west?

Yes, that is the night train going west to Halifax. The people come into town on the through train from Halifax, and it is very convenient for them to get home on this through train that goes out at 9 o'clock. There is usually standing at the town of North Sydney, an engine, and I think, a few cars, and it would not be very much trouble to make up a small train every Saturday night to run from North Sydney, about five or six miles, passing through these towns, so as to enable the people who go into North Sydney by the 7 o'clock train to return home. I think such a train would be a paying proposition; it would certainly be a great convenience to the people.
