Saturday night is pay night, the night on which people want to do their shopping, and it would be regarded as a fine stroke of business if the minister put on that local train. I trust he will give these suggestions his best attention.

I desire to add a word or
two to the criticisms made by the hon. member for North Cape Breton regarding the imperfect railway connections in the province of Nova Scotia. For instance, the Maritime Express leaves Montreal at 8.15 o'clock and arrives at Truro about noon the next day, just two and a half hours after the express train from Halifax has gone on its way to Sydney. The consequence is that persons living in certain sections of the province of Nova Scotia, off the main line of the Intercolonial, are obliged to remain in Truro for 24 hours before they are able to get a 'connection for their destination. It seems to me that some better arrangement and some better connection than that might be devised. As I have said, the Maritime Express leaving Montreal at 8.15 reaches Truro at noon the next day. It seems to me that some arrangement could be made by which that train could leave Montreal earlier, or by which it could make better time to reach Truro at 9.15 or 10 o'clock on the following day, and thus enable passengers from Montreal to connect with the day train for points to the eastern terminus of the Intercolonial railway. When the Ocean [Mr. McKenzie.!
Limited is not running between Montreal and Halifax, it takes passengers who live in certain portions of eastern Nova Scotia four days to travel from points between Ottawa and Montreal to their destination. It take>s me four days to travel from 'Ottawa to the constituency in which I live, and that is true of other hon. gentlemen occupying seats in this House, as well as of a large proportion of the travelling public who belong to eastern Nova Scotia. That seems to me to be a rather intolerable condition of affairs in this day and generation.
I fancy there is no portion of settled Canada where the people have a worse railway connection than in the province of Nova Scotia. Taking into account the fact that that province, and particularly the island of Cape Breton, has contributed so heavily towards the revenues-of the Intercolonial road, it seems to me that the Department of Railways should give to that section of the Maritime Provinces the best possible railway accommodation.
I desire to say a word or two with regard to the accommodation that is given to the public on the trains. At the present time, a passenger taking the train at Sydney at twenty minutes to seven o'clock in the morning is unable to get anything to eat until that train reaches Truro at five o'clock in the evening. As often happens, if that train is late, as was the case when I was down in Nova Scotia a few days ago, passengers who have had their breakfast at 6 o'clock in the morning are unable to get a bite to eat until 7 o'clock in the evening. Up till a year ago or so, a dining car was attached to the express from Sydney going West at Port Mulgrave, and it afforded accommodation to the passengers who desired a midday meal. When that dining car was taken off, one was attached to the day express at Antigonish, which gave passengers an opportunity of getting their meal at a reasonable time. But the dining car has been taken off altogether. I think it must be eight or nine months since there was a dining car on the day express from Sydney going to Truro. That is a great inconvenience to the travelling public. A buffet service existed on the chair and parlour cars, but I understand that even that has been cut out. It certainly was cut out on the two occasions that I travelled on the Intercolonial during the last couple of months. This is a complaint which is very general among the passengers on the Intercolonial railway. I am not making the complaint personally. In recent

months, I have not travelled very often on the Intercolonial, and I was not particularly inconvenienced by reason of there not being a dining car attached to the train; but it is a complaint which has come to me from commercial travellers and others who frequently patronize the Intercolonial railway.
There is one other matter of criticism, and that is with regard to the manner in which parlour cars on the Intercolonial railway are kept. It is a matter of very common *complaint that the parlour cars and the Pullman cars on the Nova Scotia end of the Intercolonial railway are not kept as clean as they used to be. I am not directing this criticism towards any particular official of the Intercolonial railway; I am merely stating it as a fact. I have heard ladies make very loud complaints within the last couple of months that the parlour and chair car service of the Intercolonial railway between Sydney and Halifax is not looked after as it was in the past. The complaints appear to me to have considerable foundation. As I have said, I do not'pretend to make any charges against any person in particular, but it seems to me that a little better supervision ought to be exercised by the official who is in charge of that particular department and thus remove what I regard as a very considerable ground of complaint.

Answering the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) first in reference to the port of North Sydney, I realise that it is a very important point on the Intercolonial railway. The matter was brought to my attention during the last two or three months on account of the congestion of the trade with Newfoundland.' There was a very large number of cars that could not be unloaded. Cars were detained because the boats plying between North Sydney and Newfoundland could not carry the freight on account of the large quantity to be moved. We put on one or two Government steamers in order to relieve the congestion at that point. I was also informed that this trade has grown very rapidly within the last few years. I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has been looking up the question of trade between Newfoundland and Canada, and I suppose the Reid Company, who own the Newfoundland railway, have been trying to increase -the trade between the two countries. That port has grown to be a very important one. Of course, they must have
facilities necessary to perform the work that may be required of the railway. I have not had it drawn to my attention before that the facilities were so inadequate as the (hon. member has stated. The Estimates that were made out for the Intercolonial Railway system and this, of course, is part of it, were taken up by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) at the beginning of the session. I had nothing to do with them, and I know that he cut out many important items tfhat he would like to have had in the Estimates for the Intercolonial railway on account of war conditions and the desire to keep the vote down qs low as possible, and this may have been one of them. Unless there is an item in the Estimates, the hon. gentleman knows it will be impossible for us to go ahead With the work that may be neoessary during the coming season. However, I will be very glad to look into it and see if anything can be done during the coming year to improve the facilities there. With reference to the station at North Sydney, the same thing applies. It should" not be mudh trouble to provide a little more accommodation, such as is suggested by my hon. friend, if that is all that is required, -so long as it does not involve the building of a new station.
It might be enlarged.

I will also take that matter up. With reference to the train service between Sydney and North Sydney, as I understand from the hon. gentleman, the train for Montreal leaves every night except Saturday night. As I have understood the situation in Nova Scotia, the train does not leave on Saturday night because it does not run through on Sunday.

There is a train on
Sunday night, but not on Saturday.

I know. There was a time
when they did not run right through on Sunday. I do not know whether that system prevails now, although I am aware that it has been changed in part. But, I will look into that complaint and see if it cannot be remedied. I realise that in all these large centres such, for instance, as. Sydney, people like.to get in from the country and near-by places on Saturday night., It is a very important night for people who desire to come in and do their trading, and I can see that it is quite an inconvenience if there is no train out on Saturday night. There are, of course, difficulties in operating a suburban seryice such as that which

has been mentioned for one night only. There is a rule among railway employees, in fact, it is an agreement, an understanding .with the railway unions, that if you start a crew out, even for a ten mile run, they receive a day's pay. It may be an expense that the traffic would hardly justify. But, it is well worth looking into and if I can overcome the difficulty I shall be very glad to do it. I stated a moment ago that I would like to see the people in the neighbourhood of a large centre have the advantage of coming into town on Saturday night. The large railways try to arrange a Saturday night service to enable people to get into the cities. *
With reference to what the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) stated about the train leaving Montreal for the East, the connection at Truro, and missing the connection by an hour and a half or two hours, if you start the train an hour and a half earlier you miss the connections from the west. There is one hour between the arrival of the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk trains and the departure of the Maritime Express. There is an hour allowed the people from the west to get the Maritime Express, and there is a great deal of dffi-culty in making change because if you start the. train earlier you miss the connection from the west. The hon. gentleman made another complaint which I cannot understand, but I will get the information at once. He has stated that in going west there, is no service by which a passenger getting on the train about seven in the morning can get anything to eat until five in the afternoon. There was a time, as he states, when a dining car was on, but that has been taken off, and I conclude from the remarks, he has made that there is not even a restaurant provided along the road at which passengers may get something to eat from the time of starting at seven o'clock'1 In the morning until arriving at five in the afternoon.

There is no
restaurant east of Truro.

That is what I understand,
and therefore a passenger starting at seven in the morning and arriving at Truro at five in the afternoon can get nothing to eat,, because there is no restaurant and there is no dining car service.. I think that is what the hon. gentleman said .

Quite so.
'Mr. REID: That being the case, I will take the matter up and see if we cannot

remedy this condition at once. The hon. gentleman also said that the Pullmans and the chair cars were not kept clean. Of course, any complaints of that kind, whether in this House or out of it, should be brought to the attention of the manager or of the minister, and should be remedied at once. That is one thing that must be looked after properly. It may be that those in charge of the work are not giving it the care they should.

Would it not be possible to have the train from Halifax to Sydney delayed about an hour and a half so that connection might be made at Truro? I realize that it would delay the arrival of the train at Sydney an hour and a half, and that might not be so convenient for my hon. friends who are on the main line, but those who, like myself, go over the Inverness road, have to remain over at Truro until the next day. It occurred to me that it might be possible to arrange some method by which the train from Halifax might be delayed an hour and a half, and some'other changes might be made with respect to the train from .Montreal!. I quite realize that the traffic from the West is important, and that there is only an hour between the arrival of the Western train at Montreal and the departure of the train for the Maritime Provinces. If that time were shorts ened a little, and the train starting from Halifax were delayed an hour or an hour and a half, the connection might be made. This is very important to the constituency I represent, becau.se the Inverness road is a branch of the Intercolonial. As it is at present all passengers on the Inverness road have to remain over at Truro for the night.

It is well to have all these complaints on record. I will take this matter up and see if any better facilities can be given. It might however necessitate the changing of the whole time-table. It is the wieh of the Minister of Railways and myself to give the best possible service, but it is difficult to get'a time-table . that will suit everybody. I have known us to change the time-table an hour only, and that would upset the connections with the branch line trains. We wish to have as few complaints as possible. When the manager is drawing up a new time-table I will have him look into all these com-

plainte thoroughly, to see whether any better service can be given.

If it would be of any assistance to the minister I might say something further with regard to the dining car service. It is very inconvenient as it is now. For some years the diner used to be attached to the train leaving Halifax in the morning and going east to Sydney and passengers could get their mid-day meal in the diner before the train got to the town of Antigonish. There the Sydney train going west was met, and the diner was transferred to it, about two o'clock. That was rather late, 'but the passengers had ample time to get their meal between there and Truro. If that arrangement was restored I think it would satisfy the public. I also think this way of running the diner would be cheaper than having it go through all the way to Sydney.
Railways and Canals-Grand Trunk Pacific railway-Remuneration to Government Director of $2,000.
Would the minister read the director's report?
I haven't it here.
Who is the director anyway?

Jules Hone.
Mr. GRAHAld:	He ought to be sharp.
It seems to me that if he had been a real good director he would have sent in a report to the Government covering some of the points raised in the 'correspondence with the Grand Trunk Pacific.

We have a certificate from
the secretary of the board that the director attends all the meetings.

All those he is notified
of, but I suppose the really important meetings, at which dangerous matters are dis-. cussed, he gets no notice of, I suppose he makes an annual report?
I do not think he does.

Has the minister in his
waking or other hours ever read or seen a report from the director?

I have never met the man,
I do not know him, nor have I ever seen a report from him.
Has the Minister received any report on the advisability of taking over the Quebec and Saguenay railway?

Perhaps the hon. member
could give me some information about that.

I see that L'Evenement, the Government organ in Quebec, reproduces a despatch published the night before last by La Patrie of Montreal. The proprietor of La Patrie is one of the directors of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. He announces that the arrangement is completed for taking over this 5 p.m. road and making it part of the Transcontinental, and that the resolution will be introduced in the House in a day or two. I thought the minister might be able to give me some information about that.
I cannot, for the reason that I have none. I did not even know until the hon. member mentioned it that the proprietor of La Patrie was a director of that Tailway.
He was appointed within the last three or four months.

I have no information on that. The hon. member knows the condition of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. It was started, I understand, for the purpose of serving the people living along the north shore of the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Murray bay, and is very nearly completed.
Does the minister know how many miles have been completed?
I understand that it will not take very long to complete the road and put it into proper shape.
The minister must have been getting a lot of information about the road.
Every one knows about it. If the hon. member does not want to hear any more about it, I certainly am not anxious to continue.

I am anxious to know
something about it. I will read this despatch which may clear the way for further information. It is dated Ottawa, May 2:
The fate of the Quebec-Saguenay is practically settled. The Government will present, this afternoon or to-morrow, the first resolutions to the effect of taking over the road to complete it and put it into operation as soon as possible. We do not know yet the details of the intentions of the minister beyond the fact that the Quebec-Saguenay will be added to the Transcontinental railway. This project is not included in the Bill relating to the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific.

It is a separate affair, but it is understood that it will pass. It is not expected that there will be any strong opposition.
The people of the district are naturally interested in knowing what kind of a railway it is, how many miles have been built, where it leads to, and what remains to be done. If it is to be a Government railway, I would like to know something about it.

I do not know and I do not say that it is going to become part of the Government railway system. I have no information that that has been decided upon. The hon. member has asked what condition the road is in. Our railway officials know what condition it is in.
The minister went over it.

Yes, he went over it and he knows its condition. In addition to that, Parliament has subsidized the road and has paid a large amount of money in subsidies and of course, before doing so, the Department of Railways and Canals must have had a report of the condition of the road. So far as I understand, it was the intention of the promoters of that road to run a railway between Quebec and Murray Bay and eventually it was intended to extend the road to St. Catherines bay, as a winter harbour, opposite Tadoussac. The train service between Quebec and Ste. Anne de Beaupre, a distance of about thirty miles, is owned by the Quebec Light, Heat, and Power Company, and I understand is a good paying railway.
That is an electric service.

Yes. From Ste. Anne de Beaupre to Murray Bay is a distance of sixty miles. In that locality there are many people who have been settled there for years and who have no railway service, and this railroad was intended to serve those people. Those who were building the road spent a very large sum of money on it and they got the road almost completed when financial difficulties arose and the road was not finished, although it would have taken very little money at that time to complete it. After the Minister of Railways returned from his trip over that road, I heard his statement in regard to it and I was greatly surprised as to its condition and a's to the service it would give to the people on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. The road is so nearly
[Hr. Marcil.]
completed that it is a pity to leave it in its present condition. For the benefit of the people between Murray Bay and Quebec, the road should be completed; and for our traffic between Quebec and the lower St. Lawrence during the season a road on that side of the river is just as justifiable as one on the south side. That is only my private opinion. There are, I suppose, members on both sides of the House who know the condition of that road much better than I do. I would like to know from my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) now that he has heard what I have stated, if he, knowing that locality, thinks a railroad is justified on that side of the river where there are so many people, or if he thinks the service they have had for so many years, with steamers crossing to the other side, is all that is necessary for that part of the country.

I have never been over
the road, but I understod that a railway, like any other facility, would be a good thing for that locality. It all depends upon the conditions under which the road is built. I understand that the only part of the road now being operated is in the neighbourhood of Murray bay; that from Ste. Anne de Beaupre to Quebec there is an electric service, and that a great deal of work remains to be done on the steam road. I do not know whether the Government is seriously considering the extension of the road from Murray bay to St. Catherines bay and establishing a winter port there. Winter navigation has been declared possible in the St. Lawrence by special boa^p, but it remains to be seen whether the Government will undertake the work or whether any company will be found willing to do it. We have heard of this railway being more or less of a stock-jobbing enterprise; it has been on the Montreal Exchange for a long time, the stock jumping up and down, so that the people have become more familiar with it in that way than with its real work as a railway. I do not know what amount of money has been invested in the road or whether it has been invested by Canadians or not, but I believe a large number of Parisians were glad to get their money out of it. What^I wanted to know was, as the Government papers have been announcing that the road was to be taken over, what pbs'itibn tKe road was in, so that we *yvouldbe position to criticise or to approve! 1	'

Perhaps this discussion
in regard to the Quebec-Saguenay is a little premature. The minister has given us his argument why the Government should aid * that road. Perhaps that is also premature- I do not know-but for a man who did not know anything about the road, the minister told us quite a few things, which would indicate, of course, that the Government had been studying the situation.

I said that those were the
facts in the department.
I have been in the department and I know how much study a minister would make of a special line unless something came, up specially in regard to it.

When I was acting for the
Minister of Railways, not now, but some time ago, the subsidies came due as the road was being built, and, of course, when they came up before me, I would not consent to those subsidies being paid without having a report from the chief engineer or inspector as to the condition of the road. Therefore the whole matter came before me in that way months and months ago, and I knew the condition of the road from those reports. Besides, the money spent on the road must be proved to the satisfaction of the chief engineer before amounts are paid.

That is information about the road, but it is not a reason for the minister arguing strongly for the Government acquiring the road. It has been suggested that this road can be purchased under the Branch Lines Act without the matter being brought to the attention of the House until after the purchase is made. But I would call the attention of the minister and of the Government to the fact that that could not Ibe done without treating this House unfairly, and-I say it courteously-without proper respect.
Without propeT respect?

Yes, it cannot be bought under the Branch Lines Act without treating this House without proper respect. When the Branch Lines Act was before the House the question of the railways to which it could be applied was discussed at some length; I will not read the whole discussion, but I would refer the hon. minister to page 1544 of Hansard of 1915, where he will find a few words in relation to the matter which I Shall quote. The hon.
leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had been discussing at some length this question of purchase-[DOT]
Of this road ?

No, but the purchase of railways under the Act. And he asked this question:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	We understand, then,
that this legislation applies to the Intercolonial, only?
Sir Robert Borden:	And to the Prince Edward Island railway. That is thoroughly understood.
So, that neither this railway nor any other that is not a branch line of the Intercolonial or the Prince Edward Island railway could be brought under this legislation, and the Prime Minister gave us asSUrance that it would not be done. I just bring this to the attention of the minister on account of the rumours in the corridors that this transaction has been completed under the Branch Lines Act, and that the particulars need not be brought before the House until next session if the arrangements are not completed until -after the -close of this -session. So, it cannot be done in this way without treating the House unfairly and in violation of the -assurance given by the Prime Minister.

When this question was transferred from this House to the Senate the same question was put to the -leader of the Senate, and he declared in the most emphatic terms that the Branch Lines Bill did not contemplate adding to the system of the Transcontinental, the Quebec and Saguenay, mentioning that road by name. Also, he stated mos-t positively that the Branch Lines Bill applied only to the Intercolonial. Now, we are to sit on Saturday at two o'clock. We are all anxious to prorogue and go -home. I would advise the -Government not to introduce any more contentious legislation; we already have our hands full. Not that I am against the completion of that road, but there are so many things in, and around, and behind that [DOT] road that really the Government would have to extend the sittings of this House to have considered properly.

Replying to the remarks of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), and also those of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), I anj afraid these hon. gentlemen are giving themselves , unnecessary worry about this Government undertaking to do anything behind the back of Parliament, or in con-

travention of any statute in existence. We, as my hon. friend has stated, are a Government of study. We have studied the conditions of the Quebec and Saguenay, and the situation in the West, and in other parts of Canada as well, in connection with proposed railway legislation, and when the proper time comes to make known our conclusions from that study my hon. friend need not be alarmed but that those conclusions will be made known to the House and to the country in a very open manner.
I have promised the House already to-day that any further legislation, or any further matters to be presented to this House, will be announced to-morrow.
That does not touch the point I raised.
What is that?
That if it were brought under the Branch Lines Act it would not have to be announced to-morrow.

If the hon. gentleman
had paid attention to what I said, he would have known that I said he was giving himself unnecessary worry about that.

The minister's speech
does not lessen it any.

The presence of the
Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) as leader of the House reminds me of something that happened two or three years ago. On an occasion when he was leading the House, I moved a resolution which was to the effect that in the opinion of the House the time had arrived when the Intercolonial railway with its branches should be extended into the non-railway sections of eastern Canada. The question was very fully discussed and a number of members, particularly those from eastern Canada, spoke in the debate. When we were all through, the minister, who had already spoken on the subject, accepted the resolution. The non-railway sections of eastern Canada referred to in the resolu- . tion included certain sections of Quebec, of New Brunswick, and of Nova Scotia. Since then, of course, war conditions have arisen and that is an excuse, and a good excuse I suppose, for the cutting down of large public expenditures. But when we are discussing railway matters, as mover of that resolution, and always bearing in mind that the resolution was accepted by the Government, I think it my duty to remind the hon. ministers that that ac-

eeptance on their part stands on record and that it has prevented me from introducing again a resolution of that kind. When a government solemnly accepts a resolution it assents to the acts set forth in the resolution and should at the earliest moment carry out the scheme for which the resolution was declared. I am pleased to learn from the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) that he realizes the very great necessity of giving railway accommodation to the remote sections of this country. I hope that the day is not far distant when every part of this country will have the full benefit of railway connection. I have been a member of this House for a great many years, representing the county of Victoria and the northern part of Cape Breton. In North Cape Breton we are not complaining about railway facilities; we have a railway. But in the good old county of Victoria we have no railway at all. The county of Victoria extends along the shores of the Atlantic, with its splendid fisheries, for a distance of 110 or 120 miles, but in that whole distance we have not one foot of railway. The Government of the day, in 1911, shortly before the general election, had undertaken, by legislation and by vote, to build a railway into the county of Victoria, and a resolution which I brought forward some two or three years was accepted by the present Government. That resolution involved the extension of the railroad into the county of Victoria, and I now impress upon the Minister of Railways that whenever any move is made in the direction of further railway development in eastern Canada, he will not forget that that resolution has been accepted by this House, and that the carrying out of the terms of that resolution will involve the building of a road into the old county of Victoria.

I shall be very glad, when
the matter of further extension is considered, to take up that'matter.

I should like to add my
voice" to that of the hon. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux). If the Government intends to bring in any fresh legislation we may as well make up our minds to stay here all summer, and I am anxious to get home.

I do not think there is any thing more than has been indicated by the Minister of Public Works. If there is any further legislation to be introduced it will be announced to-morrow.

Consolidation of Railway Act, $2,000.
How is that work progressing?
It is completed, I think, and Teady for presentation to the House.

How much has that
cost?
About $7,500.

With a Department of Justice, with a Minister of Justice, with a Solicitor General, with a Deputy Minister *of Justice, and quite a large number of highly paid officials on the part of that department, with a solicitor to the Railway Department, with a general counsel to the Intercolonial, why should it be necessary to go outside for the drafting of a Bill to consolidate the Railway Act? Why employ outside counsel to the extend of over $7,000, the salary of a judge of the Superior Court for a whole year, and the salary of a Cabinet Minister?

The solicitor who did this
*work was a long time at it.
They usually are.

As to going outside of the department, no man in the House knows better than the hon. member for St. John the work of the officials in the Department of Justice. They have a staff barely large enough to do the work in connection with the several departments of Government. They are all very busy, and it has always been the rule, in many important cases, to employ some outside counsel. In this case I suppose the Department of Justice had no official whom they could ask to devote his whole time to the consolidating of this Act. No Act is more important or requires more careful study than the Railway Act, and it was necessary to employ an experienced solicitor to deal with it. I think the work has been well done, and the consolidation is now ready for the House.

I am told it will be necessary for the members to watch that consolidation very closely, as in many important points a sufficient number of words have. been changed to alter the meaning of the Act. Not being a lawyer I should not know the significance of the changes, but I take this opportunity of telling legal members of the House that when the 'Bill comes up for consideration it will be necessary to investigate the changes very closely.
There is no doubt that there have been a great many changes, but I understand that the solicitor who has this work in hand consulted with the Chairman of the Railway Commission.
What is his name?
Mr. Samuel Price.
Where does he live?

He is now the Chairman of the Ontario Railway Commission. He originally came from St. Thomas. He is, from what I have learned, a very able man. At all events the work was carried on in consultation with the Chairman of the Railway Commission. When the Bill comes before the House it may be materially improved by the many able legal gentlemen who are members of this House. The consolidation as prepared will be at least a working basis, and I think it is one that will not require many changes.
Is this simply embodying into the "hew Act the amendments which have been adopted since 1903?
And any changes that may be deemed necessary in the old Act.
Reverting to the St. Peter's canal, what progress is being made with the work and when is there a chance of the capal being opened? Who is really the contractor? Is it a corporation or an individual?

The contractor is a person named W. H. Weller. He took the contract when it was tendered for, and has been working on it ever since and will complete it. I have this memorandum on the work:
The main portion of the excavation has been completed. The concrete work in the lock walls is nearly completed. Work is proceeding on the remodelling of the old lock gates which will be hung as soon as ready. By this time it is expected that the lock concrete will be fully completed and a small barrier of rock at the canal end of the lock will have been removed.
A few weeks' work in dredging out the west wall of the old lock, after the lock gates are hung will enable us to open the canal for traffic. Some minor works in the Atlantic entrance'and in the prism of the existing canal will be carried out while the canal is in service.
I understand that it is expected the canal will be open for service in the month of J uly.
What will be the depth of water on the mitre sill of the canal after the new works are completed?
We are not increasing the depth materially; it will be about 19 feet on the mitre sill at low water.

I should like to say a
word with reference to the acquisition of branch lines. The minister will remember that in 1915 authority was given to the Government to acquire branch lines of the Intercolonial. I feel particularly charged with this duty owing to the absence of the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), because I remember that he took a great interest in this question, which, as the minister knows, was first urgently advocated by the late Mr. Emmerson. In the elections of 1911, the hon. member for Kings and Albert, which two counties are equally interested in the acquisition of a certain branch line, deemed the matter of such great importance that he wired the Prime Minister, who was then in Charlottetown,
P.E.I., asking as to the policy of the Government in regard to the acquisition of branch lines of the Intercolonial. The Prime Minister wired hack to the hon. member for Kings and Albert that it was the policy of the Conservative party to acquire branch lines of the Intercolonial, and that telegram was used with great effect by the hon. member for Kings and Albert in his candidature. I do not find any fault with that hon. gentleman for asking the question, or with the Prime Minister for replying in the way he did. But I have had a good many communications sent to me in reference to the taking over of these branch lines. The people feel that the delay has been very great. I think that only two branches have been taken over by this Government. For the information of the people of the Maritime Provinces, who are more especially interested in the carrying out of this policy which was unanimously approved by both parties in the House some years ago, I would ask the acting minister whether any steps have been taken towards the acquisition of other branch [DOT] lines. I would think that before considering the acquisition of branch lines of the Transcontinental Railway, such as the Quebec and Saguenay railway, the Government ought to carry out the policy which it announced would be carried out in reference to branch lines of the Intercolonial.
The hon. member knows that we passed a Branch Lines Act.
Yes, in 1915.

Exactly; we made that step forward in order to be able to take over any

branch lines which we desired. We have taken over two branch lines, but the hon. member knows that under the present war conditions we could hardly go ahead and take over more branch lines. The fact that we have taken over two shows that we are carrying out the policy which was announced by the Prime Minister, and we will continue to carry out that policy as soon as conditions permit.

I 'quite agree with the acting minister that this is not a good time to take on new obligations, but those who have communicated with me havie heard rumours in regard to the taking over of a line which is not connected with the Intercolonial, and which was not included in the Branch Lines Act. As the minister can realize, they would naturally feel very much aggrieved if, before carrying out the policy which was approved by the House unanimously, the Government should make a new departure and take over a road which was not contemplated at the time, and which the Prime Minister, in 1915, expressly excluded from the contemplation of the Act then passed. I do not think that the people of the Maritime Provinces are anxious to have new obligations entered upon at present, but they feel that, before the Government take on 'heavy obligations in other directions, their claim ought to be considered. For instance, I had a letter the other day from a gentleman who takes a very great interest in the acquisition of branch lines in New Brunswick, which is included in the Act which was passed in 1915. He had heard rumours about large advances to the Canadian North'ern Railway Company and Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, more especially to the Canadian Northern, and he thought it would be a very great hardship upon the people of the Maritime Provinces if the Government should commit the country to further obligations with the Canadian Northern and be forgetful of the claims of the districts which are served by these branch lines in the Maritime Provinces. They feel that all parts of the country should be treated with equal consideration, and that the different railway companies should have equal justice.
Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital -Quebec bridged-construction, $3,450,000

I was to give a statement as to the Quebec bridge. With reference to that I may read a memorandum from Mr. Monsarrat, the chief engineer, dated Mont-

real, December 2, 1915. The memorandum
is as follows:
I beg to report progress in connection with the construction of the Quebec bridge for period ending November 30, 1915, as follows:
Superstructure. Since my last report the work on the north shore has progressed rapidly, and at the present time the entire cantilever arm has been completed, thus completing practically all the steelwork for the north shore, which is in accordance with the programme mapped out by the St. Lawrence Bridge Company. There still remains a certain amount of riveting and erection of sidewalk, which will be done next year.
Work has already been started on the dismantling of the erection traveller, which will be taken down and re-erected at Sillery cove, to be used in connection with the erection of the suspended span at that point.
On the south side the programme of the contractor was also carried out, and practically all steelwork completed up to and including the main post over the main pier. There still remains a certain amount of riveting to be done on this work, but this will not be done until next season. Portions of the steel falsework supporting this anchor arm are now being removed and will be used in connection with the erection of the suspended span.
Next year the south cantilever arm will be erected, after which the suspended span will be floated into place and suspended from the two ends of the cantilever arms. The work of the erection of the suspended span will be commenced early in the spring and will be completed by the time the cantilever arm is ready to receive it.
The status of the work in the shop and field is as follows:
Tons. .
Haw material ordered from the mills 69,038 Raw material received at the shop... 66,908
Fabricated at the shop	 56,145
Members delivered at the site..	..	55,434
Steel erected and partially riveted. 36,087 Net weight of erected bridge, estimated at	 65,000
Removal of unused steel. The contractor for this work entirely completed his contract [DOT] to our satisfaction.
All of which is respectfully submitted,
(Sgd.) C. N. Monsarrat, Chairman and Chief Engineer.
. I want it to be noted that this report is dated December 2, 1915, so that when the chief engineer says that the south arm will be erected next year, it means during the present year, 1916. Mr. Monsarratt told me that they are now well on with the work. The statement of expenditure is:
Total expenditure to March 31,
1914, including cost of collapsed bridge	$12,732,062 71
Expenditure to March 31, 1915	2,816,305 10
Expenditure to Oct. 31, 1915 ..	2,709,253 24

Of the above amount $10,473,346.38 has been expended on the new bridge.

I do not quite see why the minister puts into the cost of this
bridge the cost of the bridge that collapsed. We made a certain contract for this bridge, the contract was on estimated quantities and it will cost not a gTeat deal' more than the estimate, but it will cost some more. The real cost under this contract has no connection with the collapsed bridge so far as the value we are getting under this contract is concerned. When does my hon. friend expect the bridge will be completed and this span floated into position?

Mr. Monsarratt told me that he expects to (have the last span in this fall, but of course, it will not be ready for operation by that time. It is going to take some time to do the riveting and finally to complete the structure. Speaking roughly, the bridge will be completed so that you can go across it this fall if there are no mishaps. With reference to the statement of my hon. friend as to why I included the expenditure on the collapsed bridge, I merely read what is in the memorandum before me, as supplied by the officials. However, $10,473,346.38 is all that has been expended on the new bridge, and, of course, the collapsed bridge has nothing to do with it. I suppose that has been carried on in the books and they have just copied it.

I understand from the minister that they continued the construction of the bridge along the lines laid down originally by the commission. Mr. Monsarratt is the engineer, and with Mr. Monsarratt there is Mr. Snider-
A commission was appointed; I think by my hon. friend (Mr. Graham). That commission remains exactly the same except that Mr. Snider died.
Who took Mr. Snider's place?

Mr. Monsarrat said the work was so nearly completed that they did not require another commissioner, but in order to carry out the commission as elated it was necessary to appoint some one else, and, speaking from memory an Order in Council was passed appointing Mr. H. P. Borden one of his assistant engineers.
He is the secretary of the commission.
Yes.
Is Mr. Modjeska still on?
Yes.

I have no fault to find with that. The difficulty in the first place

was to got a board of engineers that would agree on a plan. After the. plan was agreed upon and the method of operation arranged for, 1 imagine they got over that part of the work for which they wanted Mr. Snider's advice particularly. Mr. Snider was one of the oldest bridge engineers on the continent, older, I think, than even Charlie Macdonald. I am glad to know that the work is going along successfully. There was a change made by the new commission in the style of the piere. Has the chief engineer reported if that has been found satisfactory?
He told me that it was found perfectly satisfactory. They were enlarged, I think.

I took perhaps a greater interest in that particular work than in anything that came before the department when I was there, because it was so difficult to get it started. I think the minister might intimate to the company that they might let members of Parliament know the day they intend to float this span into position. It is-a matter of great interest. The House ought to know that this is the largest bridge of its kind ever constructed in the world. Its completion is of great interest to the people who have paid any attention to it, and more particularly is it of interest 'to the engineering world. Each end of this bridge is being constructed separately, one on the north side, and one on the south side, and the floating span will be floated into position. It means that this span will be floated into position at a point 160 feet above high water and the work of placing it in position must not occupy much more than a few'seconds, or at all evepts a very small fraction of a minute because the tide must be taken advantage of to bring down this floating span and when it is put into position it must be put in there properly and fastened almost immediately 'or the current will take it beyond its position unless that is done. If other people are as interested in it as I am it would be a kindness to a great many if the minister would let the members know the particular day when the company intends to float that span into position, because it is something they may never have a chance to see again. That is the only point at which I tremble about the Quebec bridge, and I will sleep more peacefully at night when this span is successfully floated into position. It will re-
quire the greatest delicacy and skill. If there was still water at that point there would be lots of time to float the span in place; but as it is tidal water the work will have to be done very rapidly. Some people who have criticised this great undertaking have said that it will be impossible to accomplish it in tidal water. I want the minister to promise that he will let me know the day the span will be floated in.
I quite agree that the putting in of the last span will be a great feat, and I for one should like to see that great event.
You might take us all.

I shall be very glad indeed
to see that every member of the House gets notice of the day so that if possible we may all be there to see the last span put in. It will be very difficult to do, but Mr. Monsarrat and those who have been constructing the bridge have been so successful with the work so far, that 1 am confident that if anybody can do it they can.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Ocean and river service-P.E.I. winter mail service, $11,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is for the winter mail service to Prince Edward Island. It connects with the ice-boat service between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse. The vote is the same amount as was voted last year. The expenditure for 1914-15 was $10,996 and about the same amount was expended up to the 31st of December, 1916.
Lighthouse and coast service-construction of lighthouses and aids to navigation, including apparatus, submarine signals, and providing suitable boats for carrying on construction work, $750,000.
Is any of that expenditure to be made in relation to Hudson bay navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. The expenditure for
1914-15 was $9%,638.16. We are reducing the expenditure this year to $750,000. Up to the 31st of December, 1916, we expended $506,681.70. Out of this vote we provide all the new aids to navigation such as lighthouses, buoys, beacons, fog alarms and submarine signals, including apparatus and machinery, as well as all large repairs to existing aids and the replacing of obsolete buildings and apparatus by equipment suitable for the protection of modern heavy

draught vessels. It also includes the purchase of the plant necessary for the carrying on of the works, as well as the purchase of lands, wharves, etc., the erection of such supplementary works as may be required, the chartering of any boats that may be found temporarily necessary to properly carry out these works; the regulation of traffic in the Detroit river and such other places as may be found necessary, and the administration and operation of the lighthouse department at Prescott.
That last item looks bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, anything at Prescott is naturally bad. That includes also all the minor works which have been decided on and which will be found necessary and urgent, between the present date and the end of March, 1917. There will also be the usual work to be done in connection with the various depots, workshops, etc., together with provision for extending the accommodation at such places as will be found absolutely necessary. The expenditures for last year will be found in detail in the marine report at pages 3, and 33 to 58.
Who supplies the submarine signals?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A company that has been doing it for years, the International Submarine Signal Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There was less expended during the past year than we expected and so we have to revote a portion of the amount.
Ocean and river service-to provide for the construction of two steamers to replace the C.G.S. Quadra, $150,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A few months ago the steamer Quadra came into collision with a steamer of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company off the harbour of Nanaimo and was sunk. After getting the best opinion we could, we had the vessel sold as it lay. The estimated value of the vessel as reported by the officials of the department was $10,000. Tenders were asked for and four or five tenders were received, the highest being $9,500, or $500 less than the amount estimated by the officials of the department. We accordingly sold the vessel as it lay for $9,500. Our officials
were of the opinion that it would not pay to raise the boat and repair it as it was a very old boat and the cost of repairing it would be great. Such a boat would cost usually about $150,000. We propose to replace it with two boats, the total cost of which will be about $150,000. We find that we can discharge the service better with two smaller boats costing in the gross the same amount as the larger vessel.
Mr. MACDONALD.- Where are they to be built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In British Columbia.
Will each of those boats be a little swifter than the Quadra was?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will be swifter and better adapted for the purpose for which they are intended, that is, the lighthouse service. They are not meant for the fishery service. Speed is not an essential, but they must be properly equipped with cranes, lifebuoys, etc.

Are they to be
wooden or steel vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have not definitely decided. The plans have not been prepared.

Marine hospitals-Seamen's Hospital Fund, $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This vote of $5,000 is being given in compliance with a request made by a large delegation including some members of Parliament on both sides of the House. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and some hon. members on that side, and my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) and some gentlemen on this side, some prominent citizens of Ottawa, and some Toronto gentlemen interested in this hospital, called upon us and asked us to give a subscription of a small amount. This- hospital is situated on the Thames and is available to sailors from all parts of the world, including Canadian sailors. After these gentlemen had called upon me they furnished me with further data showing



that this hospital was rendering valuable services to our sailors who from time to time need hospital attention in that part of the world. It is a voluntary institution and among the subscribers is His Majesty the King. Over $30,000 had been raised by private subscription in Canada including a grant of $2,500 made by the Legislature of Ontario. At first, I was somewhat averse to this, but in view of the circumstances . and the desire expressed I decided to ask for this vote. Hon. gentlemen will remember that the hon. member for Guysborough brought this matter up in the House and spoke of the admirable character of the hospital and the splendid service it rendered. His views as a shipping man of experience would naturally have weight with me. After considering the matter, I thought it fair to give the hospital a grant of $5,000 to supplement the subscriptions from private sources.
Is the hospital free to all sailors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes; it is not for sailors of the navy, but for sailor,s of the merchant service.
The clairhs of the hospital were not put forward as being in any way the result of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Nor is it intended that this should form the basis for a yearly grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Not at all. I understand that in consequence of the very generous subscriptions that people have been giving for purposes connected with the war they have bad to curtail the^r subscriptions to this hospital. It is not intended that this should be an annual grant, and as I understand it there will be no occasion to ask Parliament for it again.
Fisheries-to provide for the inspection of pickled fish and the fish canneries, $25,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Fish Inspection Act came into operation on the 1st of May, 1915. Before that time copies of the Act, with the full code of regulations attached, were distributed amongst those interested on the various parts of the coast, and the general inspector of pickled fish has visited the different sections of the coast and at meetings of the fishermen and packers fully explained the requirements for putting up fish. Over one hundred of these meetings were held. A staff of local inspectors was

appointed. As the Act is not compulsory, no definite idea could be formed as to the extent to which it would be availed of at the start, and consequently as few inspectors as it was considered possible to- get along with were appointed. The Atlantic coast was divided into six districts, as follows :
1.	Cape Breton Island:	inspector, H. H.
Mann, North Sydney,
2.	The south side of Nova Scotia from Anti-gonish to Yarmouth county inclusive, inspector, A. H. Hiltz, Mahone Bay.
'3. The Bay of Fundy counties of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, including Westmorland county, N.B., Inspector, A. O. H. Wilson, St. John.
4.	The Magdalen Islands, Prince Edward Island, and Cumberland, Colchester and Pictou counties, Nova Scotia, inspector, Thomas Doyle, Rustico, P.E.I.
5.	East coast of New Brunswick, inspector, Colson Hubbard, Carafuet.
6.	GaspS Peninsula and north shore of the gulf. No inspector has yet been appointed.
As the packing of barrels for the brand increases it will be imperative to appoint additional inspectors. As the past season was the initial one under the Act, it was not anticipated that many barrels would be put up for the brand. Few of the packers had provided themselves with barrels made in accordance with the regulations. There were, however, some put up on different parts of the coast, as follows:
1,160 barrels of alewives were put up for inspection and of these, 1,158 were found to be in accordance with requirements and were branded, namely, 899 in St. John county, all of which were branded, and 261 in North Sydney, 259 of which were branded.	.
58 barrels of herring were submitted for inspection in Gloucester county, New Brunswick, of which 43 were branded.
110 barrels of mackerel were submitted for inspection, of which 10 barrels were branded, namely, 100 barrels in Kings county, P.E.I., none of which were branded, and 10 barrels in Halifax, all of which were branded.
During the last fall the educational work among the packers and fishermen was again taken up in a personal way by the general inspector. Several of the larger packers in the United States have become interested in the brand and some of them have intimated their intention of requiring all the fish they buy next season to be put up for inspection. Owing to the war the herring fishery on the European side has been reduced to a minimum, leaving the markets on this continent practically bare. The Canadian dealers are realizing this and several of them are arranging to go into the putting up of herring according to regulation next Season. One or two fish merchants went into the business last year and re-

ceived from 100 to 150 per cent more per barrel for their fish than they ever did previously. The Inspection Act, it would seem, has come into operation at a most opportune time; but the greatest care must be taken to have its provisions fully carried out, in order that the brand may become recognized on the markets as standing for the excellence of quality it indicates. If this. is not done, any trade that may be built up will be lost again when normal conditions return.

I desire to call attention again to matters of which I spoke on a previous occasion-the extension of the lobster fishing season in Northumberland straits. I was in Nova Scotia last week and saw the conditions at that time; the ice lay along the coast and fishing was not going on. The same conditions that arose last year obtain this year, and no doubt the need for an extension of the season wil-l be urged upon the minister. I am satisfied that that extension should not be given except under special circumstances; but the conditions of this year ought to justify its favourable consideration.
Mr, HAZEN:	The season does not close
until the 25th of June, and it is too early to say yet what can'be done; but we will watch conditions closely, and if they prove such that the fishermen have not had a fair opportunity to make what would be the catch of a normal year we will certainly consider the question of an extension.

I have merely taken this opportunity to accentuate what I had already said. Along the Northumberland straits for the last two or three weeks the packers have had fnen under pay and have had their supplies ready, but they have not been able to fish.
It is now the 4th of May. There is still ice all along that coast. If they do not begin fishing until next week, the minister will see that the season will be much shorter than it was agreed it should under the recommendations of the commission. Under these circumstances, where people will not have an opportunity of fishing for the period the commission recommended, it does seem to me that a case is made for an extension. I mention the matter now because I understand the minister is going away.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When representations are made we ask the inspector to investigate and make a special report for the information of the department, and we will take the same course this year.
Fisheries Marine Biological Board of Canada,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A new boat is required for the oyster culture business to replace the Ostrea which was built in 1902 and is absolutely worn out and unfit for service. The new boat is now being built at the Government shipyard at Sorel. She will be equipped with oyster dredging apparatus and will be able to do more work, and more effective work, than the Ostrea.
Some experiments were carried on in connection with the herring business last year, with headquarters at Souris. Will similar work be carried on this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Marine Biological
Board of Canada is composed of a numbeT of gentlemen, one of them an official of the department, Professor Prince, who is a specialist and a biologist, and the other gentlemen from different Canadian universities, who serve practically without remuneration, simply for their expenses. Professor MacCallum, of Toronto University, takes a great interest in this work. There are -also gentlemen from the university of Acadia, and from one or two others thoughout Canada, There is a biological station at St. Andrews and another at Prince Rupert. During this year the board has been doing very good work on the Atlantic in the continuation of experiments in the hatching and rearing of lobsters, and a continuation df the study of the natural history of the herring. On the Pacific, it has been investigating the question of kelp groves. Kelp is quite abundant along the shores of British Columbia, and it is claimed that it has very economic value , and can be used for many different purposes. The board has also been making, on the Pacific, a study of the natural history of the halibut.
In connection with the study of the natural history of	the	herring, the
services of Dr. Hjort were secured. Doctor Hjort is the director of the Nor-

wegian Fisheries, ,and is one of the most eminent experts on the herring. Keeping in view the vast possibilities of the herring fishery on this side of the Atlantic, it was considered well to arrange for Doctor Hjort's services when it was found out that such could be had last year. In order that he might be able to cover as much of the field as possible, packages of herring caught at different times of the year were procured on different parts of the coast for his examination on his arrival. After close consultation, it was considered that the end in view could best be achieved by placing at his disposal the department's steam drifter " 33 " for experimental fishing, dredging and tow-netting operations, and to arrange for two of the department's steamers to take him over desirable portions of the Gulf and Atlantic, so as to make hydrographic and other investigations. The final arrangement for these trips of investigation was as follows: Three trips were to be made in the cruiser Princess, over the Gulf, to start from Prince Edward Island and go northward to the Natashquan bank on the north shore, thence eastward to the Bay of Islands, Newfoundland, thence to St. George's bay, Newfoundland, and back to the place of starting. Three trips- in the steamer Acadia on the Atlantic coast, going over Sable Island, thence to Banquero, to Miquelon Island, thence over the Green Bank to the Grand Bank of Newfoundland, thence up to Cape Race, thence back to the point of starting. The first trips were to be made in the early part of May, when the herring and other fish were spawning and when winter conditions would obtain in the sea; the second in June when the larvae of these fish would he in the water, and the third, at the end of July or in August, when the distribution of young fish, herring, cod, etc., could he studied, and when the summer conditions of the sea are fully advanced in the different water layers (currents). Owing to the unusually late spring, it was not found possible to start as early as expected, so that only two trips, of investigation could be made, but these were carried out to the eminent satisfaction of Doctor Hjort, and in his opinion, much valuable and interesting information was obtained. The aims of the investigations were:
1. To obtain an understanding of the hydrographic conditions,-temperatures, salinities and currents.
	.
2.	To obtain material for a general description of the floating animal and plant life in the different layers of water on which the important food fish feed.
3.	To ascertain where the eggs and larvae of the different food fish are found, so as to know where they may be caught during the spawning season.
This information should throw light upon the general distribution of fishes in Canadian waters, and especially on the races and growth of the fishes. Also, important information for the same purpose was to be collected by the 313. Owing to the late date that the ice remained in the Gulf, the first trip was made in the Atlantic on the Acadia, which started on the 29th :May. The cruise was a highly successful one, the weather being favourable, enabling continuous work to be done day and night. Temperatures at different depths, and samples of water to enable the salinities thereof to be ascertained, were taken at stations twenty miles apart. The first cruise in the Gulf was taken in the Princess, starting on the 9th June. A second cTuise was made in the Acadia, over the same area as the first one, in July, and in the Princess in August. The 33 was engaged throughout the summer in carrying on fishing and other operations in the Gulf, around Cape Breton, and as far out as Newfoundland.
Associated with Doctor Hjort in these investigations were Professor Willey, of McGill University, Doctor Huntsman, of Toronto University, Doctor J. A. Mavor, of Toronto University, and Doctor Bjerk'an, a Norwegian. All the material collected could not be immediately worked up, and it was not expected that it could be completed before the end of last year or the first part of this one, so that Doctor Hjort's final report will not likely be available for a few weeks yet, but as soon as it is available copies will be printed for distribution.
I Understand that the fishing people of Nova Scotia, the Halifax Board of Trade and others who had the pleasure of hearing Dr. Hjort's addresses, * were very much pleased with the information he was able to give them, and are hopeful of very good results from the investigation which he is carrying on. He believes that the herring which visit our shores, and which are now caught near the shore, aTe not by any means the best herring, and that to get the best it is necessary to go farther out into the sea. It is to ascertain, among other things, where the schools will be found farther out in the sea that this investigation is being carried on.

Will any work of this
kind be carried on during the coming year or will this work be completed when Dr. Hjort's report is completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that the work will be completed when we get his report, in a few weeks. It may be that the report will be such that it may be considered desirable to carry on further experiments, but I do not think so, and that is the opinion of the technical officers' of the department.

If the work is finished
and the services of Dr. Hjort and his assistants will not be needed this year, I shall refrain from making a few remarks I intended to make. Otherwise I should feel it my duty to make them. Perhaps there is nothing in them, but I know that as a matter of fact Dr. Hjort, when discussing the war, was, to say the least, not antiGerman. I think it would be well, if the matter is not pressing, to suspend the work for a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think there will
be any further need for going on with it another year.

I would like to take this
opportunity of drawing the minister's attention once again to the necessity for protecting the lobster fishing industry and preventing, if possible, illegal fall fishing. When this matter was before the House on a previous occasion, the minister remarked that practically no illegal fall fishing went on during last year. I know of one case where 150 cases of lobsters without labels were offered to a buyer. The buyer did not purchase the goods, but I have no doubt that they found a market somewhere. While the labels afford a certain protection, they are not a protection against illegal fishing. What the minister requires to do is to stop the work while it is being done; that is to say, to stop the men who go from the shores, bring their lobsters in at night, and can them in the woods or in their houses. These lobsters will find a market. If they cannot sell them in the fall, they will sell them in the following season. The minister" can never hope to stop illegal fishing by simply employing cutters along the coast, distributing traps, and insisting upon labels on the boxes. He requires to have men who will be fearless in the discharge of their duties, and who, when they find men guilty of illegal fishing, will punish them severely. If this were followed up, the practice might be stopped, but I do not think you can stop it with the procedure which has been
followed for a number of years past. I kniow of this one case; I do not know if the parties were illegally fishing, but I know that the lobsters were offered for sale without labels. I do not know whether they found a purchaser or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend has a
thorough understanding of the lobster business, and his views are entitled to every respect, and will have every consideration. It is not an easy matter to prevent illegal fishing. My hon. friend knows that, during the past few years, the officers of the department have been more successful in dealing with illegal fishing than in previous years. The statement made by my hon. friend that 150 cases had been offered for sale without labels, is a serious one, and I would like the hon. gentleman to tell me, not in the House, but in confidence, who were the parties, as that might help us to guard against similar violations in future. The hon. gentleman's suggestion is, I understand, that illegal fall fishing cannot be successfully prevented by the system of patrolling the coasts, but that it is necessary to have officers, at higher salaries than are paid now, who would live outside the district altogether perhaps, appear on the scene at -unforeseen times, and perhaps catch the guilty parties red-handed. I understand that that is. what he suggests.
They would" have to be there all the time.'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If they were there all the time, the fishermen would naturally guard against them. If, as in the case of bank inspectors, they did not know when the officers might appear there would be a better chance of catching them. We will give consideration to my hon. friend's views.

The minister states that his officers have been more successful than in previous years. The reverse is the case in the province of Prince Edward Island. Some officers, I think they are called overseers, are certainly not as active there as their predecessors- were. These overseers are remiss in the discharge of their duties in Prince Edward Island.

Has the minister been in receipt of any protests from persons engaged in the lobster industry in the Maritime Provinces, soliciting his intervention with the British Government with the view of having canned lobsters omitted

from the list of imports prohibited. In former years the British market was the most important market for those engaged in the canned lobster business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have had representations of that sort. Of course, it is a matter that more directly comes within the purview of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I took the matter up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, I understand has made representations. Up to the present, no embargo has been placed upon canned lobsters, I understand, and I am hopeful that none will be.
Civil Government-Department of the Naval Service-to provide for one clerkship in First Division, sub-division " B," $2,100; to provide for one clerkship in Second Division, sub-division " B," $800 ; to provide for four clerkships in Third Division, sub-division " B," $2,000.
Mr. HAZEN; The first item is to provide for the appointment of an officer to act as assistant to the Superintendent of Fisheries. This officer is being brought in from one of the outside divisions to assist the super-j intendent in the important work of this branch; It is proposed to appoint this officer at the minimum of $2,100.
Who is he?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Ward Fisher. The
second item is to provide a vacancy for the appointment, at the minimum salary of $800 of an officer in the hatcheries branch of the fisheries. I assume that Mr. Fisher will be employed in the Fisheries Branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Entirely.
Has he any qualifications for the position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He was a fishery inspector in Nova Scotia, and his services as	such were	so extremely
satisfactory that the officials of the department recommended his appointment.

His qualifications
must have been gained very speedily be-

cause it is only within the last few years that he changed from being a fisher of men to a fisher of fish; he was a clergyman in western Nova Scotia. He seems to have been anxious to serve his country for a consideration and he is made a fishery inspector largely on account of his political activity, so I understand. What particular duties is he performing in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
His duties are to assist
the Superintendent of Fisheries. The work of the department has increased very largely. The superintendent needs his assistance in order to carry out successfully the work of his department. Mr. Fisher, in addition to being a preacher, was a newsman, and therefore is an all round man. At any rates his services are thoroughly satisfactory to the fishery officers of the department; they regard him as a very intelligent and competent man.

I would have
thought that Mr. Hockin, who was fishery officer in Northumberland straits, would have been-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a gentleman of over seventy.
I did not know that he was that old.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a pretty old man.

How old is this
gentleman of varied occupations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am told that he is 43 or 44.

^e has managed to
combine, within a very brief span, varied and interesting occupations. I fail to see, however, how he could have developed in the space of two or three years the special qualifications that would entitle him to precedence over other fishery officers in the Dominion. Some of my hon. friends from Nova Scotia who are interested in this matter would like to refer to it; or if my hon. friend has any other items perhaps he would just wait a minute.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are all the items.

Who is succeeding
him in his former position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The appointment of the
local inspector has not been made yet. It will be made in a very short time.
What are the counties in his district?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: From Halifax west.
On the south shore, or does he take in the Bay of Fundy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On the south shore and up into the Bay of Fundy. His district would take in Kings and Digby.
Has he passed the Civil Service examination?
