I regret that I was not in when the item to provide for the inspection of pickled fish and fish canneries was under consideration. May I ask the minister what is included in the provision made for the inspection of fish canneries? Has there been any appointment made in connection with this inspection, and what is the nature of the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Wherever necessary we ask our local inspectors in the different localities to inspect canneries.
That is to inspect the quality of the products of the canneries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No; the Act does not provide that. The inspection is made under the provisions of the Canned Food Act.
The Canned Food Act does not take in canned fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. The duty of administering that part of the Act which applies to fish canning establishments was handed over by the Department of Agriculture, which previously administered it, to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. We are using our1 own staff for that purpose now. We have not appointed any new officials or added to the expense in consequence of it.
Your regular officials are to pass upon how to pack the goods and give directions as to how they are to be packed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, the Act does not make any provision of that sort at all. Under the Act, their duty is to see that the operations in the canneries are carried on in a sanitary manner.
Who has been appointed to the steameT Princess which was formerly commanded by Commander Wake-ham?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Dr. Joseph Bernier.
Who is he?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He comes from Chandler,
Gaspe county, Que. Like his predecessor, Commander Wakeham, he is a physician. Dr. Wakeham was a physician when he was appointed. Dr. Bernier is a gentleman who has taken a very great interest in the fisheries, he was recommended by a gentleman in whom we have the greatest confidence and the officials of the department thought he possessed the qualifications to enable him to carry out this work in a proper manner. I do not expect that for a little while he will be the equal to Dr. Wakeham, who had a very long experience and to whom the work was a labour of love. He did a great deal of good along the coast entirely apart from the fact that he was the fishery inspector. He did much work of a benevolent and philanthropic character, and being a physician, and a very good physician, in. many cases he gave free of charge his services to people in out of the way places. I only hope that Dr. Bernier will discharge the duties, of his office in a way that will measurably compare with the satisfactory manner in which Commander Wakeham discharged his duties.

I concur in what has
been said by my hon. friend about Dr. Wakeham. His loss is Canada's loss. He was possibly one of the best officials any Government has ever had and in the distant regions of the Gulf his name is a household word. He was not only an able and experienced physician, but he was a peacemaker. On many occasions Dr. Wakeham was called in by the fishermen to settle any possible conflict arising between them, or between them and the Crown or the department. He was also exceedingly well versed in knowledge of the fisheries. He had been on several occasions requested by the Washington, as well as the Ottawa, authorities to report on the condition of the fisheries in the Gulf. No man was more interesting to listen to than Dr. Wakeham on that special subject. He was also an authority on winter navigation and on the harbour facilities of the indented coast of Labrador. In fact, I do not know how Commander WTakeham can be replaced. I have been for several years connected, politically as its representative, with the county of GaspA- I do not know Dr. Bernier personally. I wish him all success in his new career. I hope that he will never forget that he succeeds-he does not replace-Dr.' Wakeham, and that he will have

to measure up to a pretty high standard if he wishes to become the able public servant that Dr. Wakeham was.

I am very glad to corroborate in every respect what the hon. member for Rouville has said about the late Commander Wakeham. I have had the pleasure of coming in touch with him, and I know that he was a very painstaking official, probably one of the best in the department. He followed another distinguished man, the Hon. Pierre Fortin, who was the first commander of La Cana-dienne. and who established the fishery service shortly after Confederation, his work extending away up to the coast of Labrador. Both these gentlemen were of very high standing and rendered valuable service to the people along the gulf of the St. Lawrence. I hope that Dr. Bernier, who is a very young man, will be able to measure up to the position that has devolved upon him. It will be time enough to judge of his worth when we have heard of his actions. I should like to know how Quebec stands regarding the tidal fisheries. Has the licensee to pay a fee?

Baie des Chaleurs.

There is no trap fishing
there, but if there was, this , regulation would apply to the Baie des Chaleurs.
The licenses are granted yearly?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
Five dollars for the .first
ten fathoms, and 10 cents a fathom after that.

speechtext: Yes.

The last time these Estimates were up I made the suggestion that on the permanent Shell Fish Commission there should be at least one representative from the mainland of the province of Quebec. The only representative we have now is Mr. Azade Arsenault, of the Magdalen Islands, and he is not at all familiar with conditions prevailing on the north' shore of the Baie des Chaleurs, in the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure. In the last sixteeen years I have repeatedly piade the request to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for a change in the dates of the lobster fishing season. 'This industry in the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure is in a very precarious position, and has been for years past. It is claimed, whether lightly or wrongly, that the dates are not what they should be. It is well into May before the fishermen can start and they are stopped too early in the season. It is claimed that they would do better with an open season in the fall. The officials of the department have had very decided views on this and I do not think they have changed their views in these many years. I think if a competent man from the mainland of Quebec, who was familiar with the conditions, were appointed to this commission, he might be able to bring before the department the views of the residents of that locality. This Mr. Azade Arsenault is a very good man, as far as the Magdalen Islands are concerned, but they are hundreds of miles out at sea, and conditions there are altogether different from what they are in Quebec.
Railways and canals, chargeable to capital- to the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway, for a subsidy for a branch line from a point on its line as located, situated near the Spirit river settlement, to and through the Grande Prairie Land District, Alberta, for a distance not exceeding sixty miles; on the same terms and conditions as subsidies were granted in aid of the construction of certain railways as embodied in the Act 3-4 Geo. V, Cap. 96, 1913, $384,000.

I want to protect against this system of providing for subsidies. I am not arguing against the payment of this subsidy; I am rather in favour of it; I am arguing against the system that has been adopted of putting the aid to railways in the Estimates instead, as has always
been the custom so far as I can remember, of bringing them in by way of resolution upon which a Bill will be founded and finally passed. Whether designedly or not, the placing of aid to railways in the Estimates restricts the rights of the members of this House. Estimates are introduced by the minister as a message from His Royal Highness the Governor General, signed by his own hand, and every one knows that the power of a member to deal with an item in the Estimates is very limited; he can move to reduce or to strike out, but from a practical , standpoint he can make no amendment. While that objection might possibly not be serious in this case, .the aid of $15,000,000 to the Canadian Northern is put in the Estimates in this hitherto unheard of way which restricts the members of this House from expressing their views as they would like to, and of making amendments that might be made if the aid were brought down by way of resolution. The same is true with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific. There- _ fore the members of the House will have to take these Estimates and move for their reduction, or that they be struck out, or else let them go through. In the ordinary way questions of aid are introduced by wray of resolutions which have to go through a certain routine, which routine gives many opportunities to members to discuss them, to vary them, to reduce them, to change them, to make amendments in any way they like. The resolutions, after they are introduced, go before a committee and are taken up clause by clause and amendments can be made, and not one 'case out of a dozen goes through without amendments being moved' and many of them adopted. When the Canadian Northern railway resolution was going through the Government accepted amendments from this side, but here the opportunity of making amendments is veTy much restricted, and members will find, when they come to move, if they do, amendments to the aid proposed to be given to the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific that they are very much curtailed in their privileges, and unless they are prepared to reduce the aid, or to strike it out, they might as well not say anything.
Further, this method of procedure is not fair to the upper chamber, because it practically precludes that chamber from dealing with the matter at all. Whether that was the design or not, that is the result.

Estimates for money expenditures originate in this House, and, after they are passed, they are embodied in a Supply Bill, which is passed by this House and then goes to the Senate. The only power that the Senate has is to throw out the entire Supply Bill that has been passed by the House of Commons, and that would be a pretty serious matter. If a subsidy Bill were brought in by itself the Senate could discuss it, as they hawe a right to do; they could make amendments if necessary, and refer them back to the House of Commons for consideration.

I cannot agree with all that [DOT] the hon. member 'has said. - It is true that when the Estimates are brought down they must be signed by His Royal Highness the Governor General, but the same thing applies in the case of resolutions; before we can introduce a money resolution the Governor General must sanction.
That is a different matter.
No, it is an expenditure of money.
He does not sign it at all?

As to the subsidy resolutions that have been brought down for many years, the roads proposed to be subsidized were still to be built. There are often amendments made as to the conditions under which a road should be built, or the route may be changed, and so on. But the proposed aids to the Canadian Northern and the Grand. Trunk Pacific are not like the usual subsidies per mile; they are simply loans to pay interest that has been paid, or is payable, in connection with a railway that is completed and in operation.
What about this one?

I was referring to the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific first. I cannot see any objection to bringing the aid down in that way. No amendments could be made to the aid even if it were introduced by resolution. It is simply an amount loaned to the railways to pay interest and the deficit on operating expenses.

Does not my hon. friend see that if this aid were brought in by way of resolution, a member could move an amendment to the resolution that the money be given on the condition that the Canadian Northern should do such and

such things? By putting this aid in the Estimates, a member is precluded from doing that.
A member might move an amendment such as is suggested by the hon. member, but the aid is intended only to pay interest, etc. No matter what the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk Pacific may do-
It does not make any odds what the aid is for.
You might move an amendment-that, if carried, would embarrass the roads.
That is the right of Parliament.
A member has the right to move to reduce the amount.
Why did the minister not bring the matter down in the ordinary way as a money resolution?

That might have been done, but I do not see any objection to this method of procedure. So far as the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific are concerned, these aids are not subsidies at all, they are loans at a simple rate of interest, charged up to the road.

What does the minister say in regard to my other point? By putting the amounts in the Estimates, the Government has deprived the Senate of dealing with the matter except by throwing out the Supply Bill, which covers all the money required for all the purposes of Canada for the coming year.
They cannot throw those items out without throwing out all the other Estimates.

Is not that a perfect answer to the remarks made by the minister a few minutes ago, and does not it support the contention of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), that when any moneys are being voted for a special purpose that should be a matter of a special Bill, because it may be subject to a variety of amendments to which hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House may agree? No one cares very much whether the aid is brought in by way of resolution or by placing an amount in the Estimates, so far as the early stages of the matter are concerned, but it should pass through Parliament in the form of a Bill because it is special legislation. I submit that the

' remarks made by the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew are perfectly correct, and they have not so far been answered.
I do not agree with the hon. member that the Upper House would throw this out.	.

We did not insinuate
that it would.

The conclusion I draw from
the remarks of these hon. gentlemen is that perhaps that would be the result.
Even though they concur in these votes for $8,000,000 and $15,000,000 I would still say that this is not the proper course to pursue.

We will have to agree to
disagree on the subject of procedure, so far as these items are concerned. But as to the item now before the committee
That is a subsidy.

Yes, that is entirely different from the other two. This is a subsidy for the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway for a branch line, from a point on its line as located, situated near Spirit river.t I may explain that the matter of railway facilities for the handling of grain produce and supplies required by the settlers of the Spirit river settlement and through the Grande Prairie district of Alberta was brought to the attention of the Government, and it was decided that, as the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway Company had a charter to build a line to these districts, a vote should be given to cover a line sixty miles in length, the same to be given under the conditions of a subsidy granted under the Subsidy Act. A few words in answer to the hon. member for South Renfrew. If I remember well, last spring the question was brought before the Minister of Railways of having this sixty miles of railway completed at once, for otherwise the large quantity of wheat in that section could not .be brought out. After the facts had been laid before the minister, and an assurance given by the railway company that they could not complete the railway without a subsidy, he agreed to give them a subsidy for this line. The reason why it is put in this form is that the Minister of Railways had decided that this year, vowing to war conditions, he would not bring in a subsidy Bill.
But he grants this subsidy.	,

This is really for last year.
Many subsidies have expired the renewal of which is asked for, and some want new ones. But this vote is made to assist in getting the grain out of that country during the past season, and, as we are not having any regular subsidy Bill, the amount was put in the Estimates to carry it on the terms here mentioned. It was simply because of the promise the minister had made that we would not have a subsidy Bill that this is proposed in this form. Of course, if there had been other subsidies, a regular subsidy Bill would have been introduced.

I want it clearly understood that I am not dealing with these items because they are these items, but I am objecting to the principle on which they are submitted to Parliament, and I am taking the earliest possibility opportunity of doing so. The principle is wrong. As explained by the Acting Minister of Railways this subsidy is put in this form merely to protect the Minister. of Railways against the direct violation of a promise, but it protects him only by violating that promise in an indirect way. He told applicants that he was not going to have any subsidy Bill, and they, of course, thought he was not going to give any subsidies-for that must have been the idea they took away with them. He now proposes this way of giving a subsidy which ought to be given through a Bill.
This was earned.

The minister is not to be excused for violating his pledge by bringing this subsidy in, as it were, by the back door. I want to go on record as objecting to this as a yiolation of a principle. If this is to be made a precedent hon. members on either side are going to be deprived of opportunities which they now enjoy to deal in a practical way with matters of this kind, and the Senate will have practically nothing to say about aids to railways or anything else. These things ought to follow the safe parliamentary practice and ought to go through the regular appointed stages. A money measure has to go through stages which other Bills have not to follow. The measure is first brought down in the form of a resolution, and then a Bill must be introduced founded on the resolution, and the Bill cannot be altered materially from the resolu-

tion on which it is founded. The Bill must go through first, second and third readings and be passed by the House, and then must be sent to the Senate. Ample opportunities are afforded for hon. members to discuss the measure and to deal with it, and of those opportunities they will be deprived if these subsidies are allowed to go through in the Estimates.

The hon. member is quite
right as to the procedure, and there is no desire to vary that procedure. But this item, as I have said, was agreed upon long ago, and the minister informed the officials of what had been done. Many other lines, in the Wefst particularly, are asking for subsidies, and man/ of them ought to be granted subsidies as soon as we are in a position to do so. But, as we are not able to take them up this year, and as this is the . only item, we thought that under the circumstances not much fault could be found with it. When more subsidies are to be granted, I have np doubt the minister will bring them in in the regular way as outlined by the hon. member for South Renfrew.

This particular item relates to a railroad development in the constituency I have the honour to represent. From the discussion that has taken place it will be apparent to the committee that there probably appeared to the Government to be some special reason why this aid should be given. I desire, if I may, to take a little of the time of the committee to explain the railroad situation in that part of the country. In that explanation will appear, to some degree, from one point of view at any rate, the reason for this special aid. The minister has already stated that there was a settled and productive area having a surplus of product which had to find markets, or the people had to go broke. It was a matter of extreme urgency to give that settlement railroad facilities during this season. Circumstances were such that it was possible to give facilities, but it was necessary that substantial assistance should be received, and the minister has said that a promise was made that this assistance would be giveh. At any rate, I wish to inform the House that whatever the minister has said here to-night in regard to the desirability and the urgency of the construction of this piece of road is absolutely supported by the facts. I have pleasure in informing the House that the rails have

actually been laid, and that although the line has not been ballasted, traffic is now being carried over this piece of road, to the great advantage of the large and important and productive settlement that it is intended to relieve and to connect with the outside world. But I think it would not be fair to the House or to the country, and it would certainly not be fair to my constituency, if I did not take this opportunity of placing before the House the general reasons which led up to this proposed subsidy. It will be within the knowledge of those who have followed the question, that during the great rush of immigration and expansion that took place in the prairie regions of the West in those better years before our friends took office, the prairie area of the Saskatchewan country was practically occupied; it had been practically alienated; it is now in private hands, not in the bands of the Government. There are still vast areas of timbered land or partially timbered laqd available for settlement, but there are practically no prairie lands available in the Saskatchewan country, speaking of the southern part of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. But there is in the Peace River country, in northern Alberta, a number of prairie areas of a very desirable character which have attracted settlers to such an extent that they have gone in to a distance of 300, 400 and 500 miles, over roads through wooded country, and have opened up the country, established farms, created production, and carried that production to such an extent in the case of this Grand Prairie, and in other areas that I desire to mention, that they cannot go any farther unless they can get aq outlet for what they have produced. The Provincial Government, recognizing the needs of the people who had already gone into the country, entered upon a policy of railroad guarantees with a view of ensuring the productive development of this Peace river country. A federal charter was held and was acquired by one J. D. McArthur, a charter under the name of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway Company. This charter was to carry a line from Edmonton to the British Columbia boundary, passing a few miles south of the main stream of the Peace river, at the point Dunvegan. The company were fortunately able to realize on the guarantee of the Provincial Government to an extent that enabled them to carry their construction as far as Spirit river, 357 miles from Edmonton, 15 miles

south of Dunvegan on the Peace river, into the centre of a very desirable prairie area known as the Spirit river prairie. But at that point the railroad was 50 or 60 miles from the central point of the Grand Prairie, a large prairie area and was really of no very serious value to the settlers on the Grand Prairie. Certainly it was an advantage to have a railroad within 60 miles instead of 300 miles, but as a matter of actually producing grain and selling it at a profit, the railroad might just as well have been almost anywhere else. The Provincial Government gave a guarantee for this 60 mile branch to Grand Prairie, but in the present condition of the world's finances I presume the company would have had difficulty in financing for the construction of that road, had it not been for the assistance promised by this Government.
The Peace river itself is one thing; the Peace River country is another thing. The Peace river itself is a large and navigable stream, navigable for a stretch of 500 miles, from the foothills of the Rocky mountains to the chutes below Vermilion, and on each side of that river there are large prairie areas which we speak of as the Peace river country, areas which are desirable for settlement and which attract settlers by reason of the fact that they are prairies. A settler going into occupation, of these areas does not have to clear his land and does not have to wait so long for production as if he went into the wooded country. Because of this advantage of getting prairie land, the settler is willing to travel far from railroad communication. He is willing to undergo certain, hardships, finding his compensation in the advantage that he does not have to clear his land of timber or wait many years for the clearance to take effect so that he can get crops. That is the reason why the Grand Prairie was settled so far in advance of railroad construction.
But there are other areas in the Peace river country also which have been settled in advance of railroad construction, and it is to the condition of these areas that I desire to call the attention of the House and the Government for present or future consideration. On the north side of the Peace river, extending from Peace river crossing for a distance of sixty miles to Dunvegan, is another area of beautiful prairie country, occupied by settlers, producing largely, and still, so far as the main line of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway is concerned, just as far from reach of the actual advantages, of railroad communication as the Grand Prairie was, because these people are on the opposite side of the Peace river, and the valley of the Peace river is a tremendous impediment to travel, being a valley 800 feet- in depth. In order to reach the navigation of the Peace river-because it will be observed that the route of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway did not contemplate reaching the actual valley of the Peace river-and at the same time approximately reach this large settlement on the north side of the Peace river, the Provincial Government, or possibly this Dominion Government, chartered a branch line of railroad leaving the main line of the Dunvegan railroad at McLennan Junction and reaching the Peace river in a distance of fifty miles. The charter, I believe, carries the railroad across the river, and the Provincial Government gave this branch a guarantee of $20,000 a mile, the same as in the case of the main line and the Grand Prairie branch. But the railway company was unable, under present conditions, to market the bonds, even with the Provincial Government guarantee. The Provincial Government believed it was so urgently necessary that that railroad should reach the navigation of the Peace river, and give approximate advantages of railway connection to those settlers on the north side of the river, that a year ago the Provincial Government raised a loan on their own credit, and then gave a loan to the railway company of 80 per cent of the actual cost of construction of that 50 miles, in order to link up the 500 mile stretch of navigation on the Peace river with the railroad system of Canada at Edmonton. As the result of the action of the Provincial Government in making that loan, the company has been able to construct that 50 miles of road, and the rails to-day are either actually at the bank of the Peace river or within a mile or two of it. At any rate, by reason of the action of the Provincial Government in guaranteeing the bonds of the railroad from Edmonton to McLennan, and by making an actual loan of 80 per cent of the cost of construction from McLennan to Peace River Crossing, the country has the advantage of the linking up of the navigation of the Peace river with the railroad system of Canada, and the settlers on the north side of the Peace river have the railroad brought at any rate to one end of the

settlement, the river intervening between them and the railroad.
Tip to the present, then, the situation is that by guarantees amounting to $8,000,000, and by a loan, which I will estimate at $1,000,000, with aid from this Government to the amount, approximately of $300,000 in cash, there has been opened up to settlement that great Peace river country. By the use of the credit of the Provincial Government, we have 400 miles of actually constructed railway, which is absolutely necessary to bring that country within range of profitable and actual settlement. -With the assistance of this Government we have 50 miles more, bringing another large important productive area within the range of railroad communication. What I want to bring to the attention of the House is this: The Provincial Government has put up, as I have said, $9,000,000 in credit and cash for the development of the Peace River country, as far as it has yet gone. This Government has put up between one quarter of million dollars and half a million dollars, or will do so when this vote is passed. Now let me point out that the responsibility for the development of the western country does not rest properly upon the provincial governments. It does rest properly on this Federal Government. It is the Federal Government that owns the land, the timber, and the minerals. It has absolute control and ownership of all the natural resources of that country, and it is recognized to be responsible for its settlement and development by the control and direction of immigration. It may be asked, why did the Provincial Government go so far in order to secure that development for which it was not responsible. The Provincial Government is responsible to the people who are there. The people had gone into that country, in spite of all the difficulties, and they turned to the Provincial Government and said, you must give us assistance in ordeT to enable us to live in this country into which we have gone. The Provincial Government is responsible to that extent, but I desire to lay before the House my opinion, and I do so without consultation with the Provincial Government. I am responsible for the representation of the constituency in this case. In my judgment, the Provincial Government has gone approximately as far as it can go in that work. Whatever their intention or desires may be,
I do not conceive that the Government of the province of Alberta can continue indefinitely to guarantee railroad bonds and expect that guarantee to remain of serious

value. A time must come when, if the. guarantee is continually extended, it will be reduced in actual value, and therefore be of no effect.
I desire to take this opportunity of saying to this House that in my judgment the responsibility for securing the development of the Peace River country, as well as of all the new countries of the West, rests primarily upon this Government; and while giving this Government credit for the aid it has given in this case, I propose, so far as I can, to place upon it the full responsibility for the further development of that country, and to come right down to details and make certain suggestions, if I have the privilege of doing so.
The suggestion I make is this: The railroad having reached the eastern bank of the Peace river, in order that the country on the west side of the river may be developed-a country, remember, 500 miles in length; 200 miles up stream to Hudson's Hope at the Rocky Mountain portage, and 300 miles down stream to the chutes below Vermilion-it must have railroad communication. You pannot have profitable production and development without railroads. Therefore, a railroad must get across that river before we can see the development of that country. On the west side of the Peace river, as I have said, there are 60 miles of solid settlement, and there is no better settlement in. the Dominion than that which lies north of the Peace river. Those people just as urgently need railroad facilities as did the people of Grand Prairie last year, but there lies between them and the present railroad terminus on the right bank of the river the width of the river, with the difficulties of climbing the hill on the west side over and above the ordinary cost of constructing a line of railway through level country. I have not consulted	engineers on	the	subject,,
but my information is that the Peace river is a stream 1,800 feet wide at high water, that it has depth approximately of 16 feet in the channel at low water, that it has a rise of 20 or 30 feet and that ice forms in the winter of not less than 4 feet in thickness. It is evident that to construct a permanent bridge across such a stream is a great and costly work and a work of such a tremendous character that no provincial government could reasonably be expected to finance it, nor could any colonization railway company. If the railroad being built in the Peace river country were of a transcontinental character, then we might

say that the company would be able to finance such a bridge, but a branch road to Peace River crossing is not a transcontinental project, it is purely a colonization project and, stating my own opinion only and not having consulted the company, I cannot imagine that a colonization railroad being backed only by a province, which already has guaranteed railways very largely, is likely to be in a position to finance the cost of a bridge to be built at that point. It would- be a calamity if money were spent in putting a bridge across that river at that point that. would not be of a substantial character. If a company with limited resources, or with limited backing, undertakes to put a bridge across there, it may be tempted to take a chance and make the same error as was made in the case of the Quebec bridge, by having light construction instead of heavy construction with the result that the whole expenditure may be lost. This Peace River Crossing is a geographical strategic point. It is the natural gateway to the Peace river country and any bridge that is built there might very well be built for all time, to use a common expression, and consequently should not be built to be held in the hands of any single railway company to the exclusion of any other company that might wish to enter the Peace river country by that route. Therefore, my suggestion to the Government is that in due course they recognize their responsibilities in the development of the Peace river country, the necessity of railway connection and, particularly the necessity of railway extension across the Peace river, and that they either assume the responsibility of putting a railway bridge across the Peace river at that point or give - such a substantial subsidy to a railway company as will enable the company to put a bridge across	the river
there that	will be a	thoroughly
substantial and reliable bridge, such bridge to be for any other railway company that may desire to cross the river there, subject to reasonable charges for upkeep or use.
Following the construction of .the bridge comes the question of rising out of the river valley. A rise of 800 feet of clay bank necessarily means very expensive construction. I would think that, in addition to the construction of the bridge, there might very well be considered the question of assisting the railway financially to rise out of the valley by a reasonable grade. At
that point, in getting down to the river valley oil the seat side, the railroad company has at present a grade of about 3 per cent or perhaps a little over. That is an abnormal grade. It is not a good working grade for hauling heavy traffic but it is such a grade as was possible with the money that was available. It enabled the company to get their road down to the river practically last fall when, if they had tried to get a lighter grade, they would probably not have been there for a year or two yet. But in any case the problem of rising out of the river valley is a serious one and I would suggest that the Government might very well take that into consideration, in recognizing their responsibility for the development of the country west of the river.
The main thing, the immediate thing, is the construction of the bridge and I would certainly say that aid at the hands of this Government towards the construction of such a bridge' as that might very well go to the amount of $1,000,000. If it were settled that this Government would make itself responsible for the construction of the bridge across the Peace river then settlement would go in west of the river and occupy the prairie all the way from the crossing to Hudson's Hope, a distance of 200 miles, because people would feel that there was a probability of getting railroad communication within a reasonable time. But, with that tremendous river unbridged, there does not appear a reasonable possibility of railroad construction on the west . side of .the river and therefore it is a great ' drawback to settlement because settlers under these circumstances will not go in and occupy the country.
There is another settlement that I wisji to draw attention to in this connection. I have been speaking of a point entirely within my own constituency. I desire to speak now of a settlement that is not within my own constituency, but which immediately adjoins it. Under the arrangements by which British Columbia entered Confederation, in some -way in consideration of the building of the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Government acquired 3,500,000 acres of land in the Peace river country in British Columbia. It is called the Peace River Block. The area has been set apart, it is administered insofar .as the land ownership is concerned by this Government but it is under the jurisdiction of British Columbia. The Edmonton and Dunvegan railway charter reaches the

British Columbia boundary at this Peace River Block. The Government of Alberta has guaranteed its bonds to that point. Immediately west of the British Columbia boundary, in the Peace River Block, is a settlement called. Pouce Coupe, a, beautiful prairie area that is entirely occupied by settlement. There are about four townships of solid settlement on this Pouce Coupe prairie.	It is GO miles distant from Spirit river. A preliminary survey of the railway has been made, the charter has been granted, the bonds have been guaranteed, but I presume that the construction of the railway for that distance will	be	in very much
the same position as the construction of the line to Grand Prairie; that is to say, the guarantee will hardly be found sufficient to enable the company to finance the construction of that piece of road. Now the settlers are there; many of them have been there for four or five years; they are producing on a very considerable scale; and it is necessary that they should have railway communication, or they cannot continue to produce. If we want to increase production in this country-and I understand that that is what we do want-surely it is our business to see that where the people are on the land, and production has been undertaken, the railroad facilities should be provided that are absolutely necessary to success in the matter of production.
Let me go a step further and discuss this question of railroad extensions and of aid to railways. At the present time there is a considerable feeling that Canada has gone too far in railroad building, ibas spent too much money, and that we should restrict our efforts in that regard in the future. I do not want to argue the question from the point of view of those who hold that idea, but from the point of view of the man upon whose exertions and upon whose success the future of this country absolutely depends; and that is the man who has gone out beyond the frontier of present settlement, in order to bring into cultivation and production land that without his enterprise and without his labour would be of no value either to this country or to anybody else. That man cannot succeed unless he gets railroad facilities; he cannot provide those facilities for himself; some one must provide them for him, or he cannot succeed. And naturally and necessarily it is to the great mass of t'he people at large, who aTe looking for their prosperity to the de-velopmentr of that area the settler is
[Mr. Oliver. 1	1
occupying-it	is to the nation at
large that we must look for the financial risk that must necessarily be taken by somebody in order that that man may have the possibility of success brought within his reach. We may have over-built in some particulars, we may have over-spent in some particulars, we may have shown lack of good judgment in some particulars; but when a man has severed himself from the associations of his lifetime, and taken his wife and children out into the wilds, fifty or a hundred, a hundred and fifty, or two or three hundred miles away from those facilities which necessarily go
10 p.m. with railroad communication, and is fighting the battle with nature-for his own benefit, it is true, but still for the nation at large-it is no use telling that man what you have done in other places. What you must do is to provide that man with railroad facilities, or he cannot succeed, and then you cannot succeed because he did not succeed.

I do not know that I have much fault to find with what my hon. friend from Edmonton has said in regard to conditions in the northwestern portion-of the province of Alberta. As a western representative, I am one of those who believe that this Parliament has never yet fully recognized the importance of the development of the great prairie provinces of western Canada. It is true that in the early stages of .construction assistance, by way of land grants, -and so on, was given to the Calgary and Edmonton, and the Regina and Long Lake railways, and, perhaps,- one or two other branches in the Prairie Provinces. But for many years no assistance had been given towards the construction of railways in any one of the three Prairie Provinces, except that this Parliament seemed to recognize the great importance of the construction of transcontinental railways, and, contributing in that direction, had probably brought about the construction of one transcontinental railway too many. The fact remains that the local development of railways in the Prairie Province of the West has not in the past received proper consideration from the Parliament of Canada. For example, it was very necessary about the year 1900 that the people living in what was then know as the Northwest Territories, west of the province of Manitoba, should have an outlet to lake Superior for the transportation of their grain. There

was a pressing need for this; railroad rates were so high that it was almost impossible to hope for the development of that western country without providing cheaper means of transportation for its products. When the Government of the province of Manitoba undertook to remedy this condition, they found that it would be necessary for them not only to guarantee bonds for the construction of lines in several directions within the borders of the province, but also to guarantee the construction of a line in Ontario for a distance of something like 290 miles. They gave the guarantees; the road was constructed, and freight rates were brought down by something like 4 cents a bushel or 4 cents a hundred pounds -I forget which [just at the moment- which was of great benefit to the people of. western Canada. This policy of guaranteeing bonds of railways was followed by the new provinces when they were created; it was followed by this Parliament shortly afterwards, in the construction of the Transcontinental. The item now before us is, I think, the first direct grant by this Parliament in the last twenty years, to any branch line in any one of the three Prairie Provinces. 'I endorse what my hon. friend from Edmonton has said as to the necessity not only of this grant, but of additional grants for the purpose of bringing about the construction of branch lines in the different provinces of the West; and in no section of the country, I think, is there greater need for such assistance than in the Peace River district west of Edmonton. We have there what is recognized by every one who has studied the possibilities of that country practically an empire in itself. We have millions upon millions of acres of the finest land that can be found in probably any part of the civilized world; and having to-day three transcontinental railways, none of which has a sufficient amount of traffic to maintain it as it should be maintained, we must see to it that feeders are constructed in the various provinces to supply those railways with additional traffic, thus relieving this Parliament of being called upon year after year to grant aid to those railways. Were it not for the war conditions and the circumstances which exist at present, I am free to acknowledge that, if the matter were in my power, this Parliament would be asked to continue to subsidize in a large measure the construction of railways in the Peace river district, as well as in other districts in Western Canada. The present conditions are the only reason why this Parliament is not 218
asked even at this session to give assistance towards the construction of those lines of railway. There is this justification why those lines should be built, that the people of Canada own and control all the lands in all the provinces in the West; that they own and control all the timber and all the minerals, and in that respect those provinces are therefore differently situated from the other provinces of Canada. Consequently it is our duty and responsibility to assist in the construction of those lines for the development of those great prairie provinces, and, above all, for the development of the Peace river country, where we have such magnificent possibilities. I trust that in the near future this Parliament will recognise its duty towards Western Canada in this respect.
As regards the criticism offered by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) as to the manner in which the Estimates for the assistance and loans proposed. to be given to the Grand ' Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern have been presented to Parliament, it is quite true that perhaps the common practice in, this Parliament in the past has not been followed. I would, however, like my hon. friend and other hon. members to understand that conditions are entirely different from those which have existed in former years. We find it necessary, on account of war conditions, in view of the heavy responsibilities involved, to keep those railways from defaulting; and in view of the heavy assistance which has been granted in the past, we have been obliged to place in the Estimates a further item of $150,000 to provide for an inquiry into the general railway system of Canada to consider the advisability of the nationalization of 'those two railways in particular, and probably of other railways in the Dominion as well. This is an important undertaking, and the items in the Estimates represent simply temporary assistance that this Parliament would be obliged to give were we to take over those two railways to-day, and until we have made a thorough investigation into the general railway system, we do not know whether that might or might not be the best course to pursue. With a national system of railways in Canada, we in the prairie provinces of the West would have reason to hope that this Gov-eminent would recognize the importance of that great territory, and that it would secure the construction of the additional branch lines so necessary for its develop-



ment and to make profitable the great transcontinental railways that' are already in operation. That is the position we take. We have introduced the items in this form and when they are reached they will be discussed in the House by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance in detail, and the House and the country will be given every particular that they should or could expect to receive.
I want to assure my hon. friend from South Renfrew and this House and the Upper Chamber that there never was a thought, and I never heard it mentioned by any of my colleagues, either in, council or elsewhere, that by the introduction of these items in the Estimates, the powers of this Parliament or of the Upper Chamber might be curbed in any way, and I would not wish to have any misunderstanding about the matter. We acted in the manner in which we did, giving a direct and temporary loan, in order to maintain the conditions that exist to-day, believing that it would not be desirable at the present time to allow any default to take place, especially when we have in view the wider idea of bringing about the nationalization of the railways of Canada, with a view of ending, once and for all, this procedure of the coming to Parliament, from year to year, by the various railways of Canada, asking for assistance. I am sure when the matter is explained in detail, it will meet with the approval, not only of this Parliament, but of the Canadian people as a whole.

I wish to draw attention
to what appears to me to be a very serious situation, to relieve which, some measures should have been taken by the Government during the past winter. He gives a statement of the sto.eks of wheat in Canada on March 31, 1916. It is as follows: Terminal elevators, 25,528,440 bushels.

That is at Port Arthur or
Fort William?

Yes. Hospital elevators,
534,876 bushels. Winter storage in vessels, 2,447,386 bushels; that would be at Fort William. Inter-terminal elevators of the Dominion	Government-Calgary,	629,956
bushels; Moosejaw, 2,820,523 bushels. Saskatoon, 1,632,692 bushels; interior terminal elevators of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Transcona, 633,327 bushels. It appears to me that a situation which finds us at the opening of navigation with two-thirds of our total crop still in" our own country, when we must look to market at least two-thirds of it across the water, is a very serious one; and, while I do not wish to harshly criticise the Government, it seems to me that it is a situation which should have been recognized earlier in the season. To repeat what has been said already, instead of the Government being satisfied with utilizing the storage capacity at Quebec and Montreal, which was, of course, in itself, very desirable, there should have been the most strenuous efforts to rail haul as much of that wheat as possible to tide water and to get it across the ocean during the past winter. Unless the wheat is carried across the ocean very much more rapidly during the coming summer than it was during the past winter, the next crop will find us with a large part of this wheat still within the country, and therefore not actually realized upon as it must be if the financiaL condition is to be properly maintained. I certainly cannot help thinking that the Government has not recognized to the full their responsibility when they had available the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to handle an enormous quantity of that grain to the ocean ports during the past winter. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said and repeated that it was not possible to get that grain shipped across the ocean during'the past winter. If it was not possible during the winter, there is no reason to suppose that it will be more possible during the coming summer. The urgency of getting the grain forward over the railroads should certainly have been supplemented with an equal effort to get it across the ocean. The situation is so very .serious that I do not apologize for bringing it to the attention of the House and of the country, or for placing a very serious measure of blame upon the Government which has the fullest responsibility in the matter and, in some degree, the control of the situation in its hands.

The hon. member is absolutely right so far as the seriousness of the matter is concerned, but as I stated before, and as his own argument shows, the Government were powerless to do more than they did. If you. could not get it across the ocean, you could not do any more than fill the elevators at this end. The next difficulty that the Government was up against was this:	It was intended when
the Transcontinental railway was started that the Grand Trunk would have engines and cars ready to operate it, but they only had equipment for the western part of the road. I explained 'why we could not do more work with the Transcontinental and the reason I gave them is the reason I give to-night, that we did not have sufficient equipment. Then I was met by hon. gentlemen from the lower provinces who criticised us because we took 75 engines and a number of cars from the Intercolonial. They claimed this was an injury to the Maritime Provinces. Seventy-five engines are nothing on such a long road as the Transcontinental. But we hope to be in a better position next winter because we are ordering a large number of cars and engines to handle the western crop in a much more satisfactory-way than we have done during the past winter. It takes time to get the equipment and organization necessary to handle the western crop. I am quite sure that everything was done that could have been done although there is no doubt that much more was required to meet the demand for the transportation of grain from the West.

One reason why I am so insistent in bringing this matter to the attention of the Government is that we have two lame-duck transcontinental railways on our hands. The assertion is made very frequently, and is generally accepted, that the reason these are lame ducks is that we have not sufficient business for them to carry. I desire to say that we have the business that should have been carried by these roads during the past winter, in which case they would have served the purpose for which they were created, and I presume that, had they done this businss, they would have helped to carry themselves to a certain degree. Therfore, the argument that we have not the business does not stand on a sound foundation. But the other alternative is that those who are responsible for

handling the business have not discharged their duties with success or credit. I do not wish to press that point, but it has to be one way or the other. There is no doubt that we had the business this year. Perchance we will not have it next year because the fact that we were not able to handle the business this year satisfactorily necessarily restricts production for the coming year; so that we have made a double loss by not being able to handle the business we had in hand during this past year.

s
that Pullman cars would be needed on the Transcontinental. The order for these cars should have been given a year ago, im; mediately the Government took -over the road. Why did you not ask for it? You passed legislation last winter by which you took the right to take over that railway.

We took the right, but the matter was not decided until after the session. According to the Grand Trunk Pacific Act, that company were to have equipment for operating the Transcontinental when it was completed, and we believed that they would have a certain amount of equipment that we could get from them; but when we took over the Transcontinental, we could not get any equipment of any kind, and, therefore, we were compelled, in order to operate it as we have been doing, to take the equipment from the Intercolonial in the meantime until we could furnish more equipment. With the orders which we have given and which will be given, we are going to have a very large amount of equipment which will be used on the whole Government railway system.

Then the real reason for the congestion of traffic and the interference with transportation on the Intercolonial this winter has been that the equipment of the Intercolonial was taken for the Transcontinental.

It is hardly fair to put it
that way. That, of course, was one reason why we could not have a better service on the Intercolonial. In addition to that, the amount of freight traffic was very large on the Intercolonial this year; in fact, there has never been anything like it in. the history of that railway. I had the figures here

a few minutes ago and the increase in freight traffic was enormous. The passenger traffic was also much greater because of the large number of troops carried over the Intercolonial this year, and on each troop train we had to use two engines. In that way both the passenger traffic, on account of the troops, aud the freight traffic made the traffic on the Intercolonial so enormous that even that alone might have prevented the local traffic from receiving the same service as it had in the past.

The minister then
admits that his' general manager did not foresee this additional traffic; that he took the equipment in order to operate the Transcontinental and that caused the congestion. Would the minister he good enough to tell me whether he has directed that the lower rates be given to the soldiers who have volunteered for overseas service? I asked him about the matter before the Easter vacation, and I understod that it was carried out, but I found out that it had not been done until a few days ago.

I took the matter up with
the general manager and I understand the notice has been sent out. I telephoned to the secretary of the department to-night, and he advises me that soldier- on furlough and on public holidays can get return tickets at single fare, that the management was so instructed, and that the rate went into force on Good Friday. The soldiers must present certificates from the commanding officers.

Is the Valley Camp Coal Company of Fort William supplying American coal?	[DOT]
Yes.

And is there any
other supplying American coal to the Intercolonial?

Bailie and the Nova Scotia
Steel Company, I think, supply Montreal too. It is possible they will have to bring some American coal as well. They have the right according to my recollection if they cannot get the coal in Canada to supply American coal.
And what about Bailie at Quebec supplying the Transcontinental?

Is that the Canada Import
Company? I do not know who manages that.

Can they give
American coal?

If they cannot get Canadian. We are taking all the Canadian coal we can get, and if we take American it is only because we cannot get the Canadian coal delivered. The hon. gentleman knows the coal situation in the lower provinces. They are giving us all they can spare for Montreal. There is the difficulty of getting it
